Emergent Gauge Flux in Mixed QED3 with Flavor Chemical Potential: Implications for Magnetized U(1) Dirac Spin Liquids

October 31, 2026
Abstract

We design a lattice model of a “mixed” U(1) gauge field coupled to fermions with a flavor chemical potential and solve it with large-scale determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations. In this mixed construction, dynamical magnetic monopole events are suppressed in the temporal-continuum limit. For zero flavor chemical potential, the model realizes three-dimensional quantum electrodynamics (QED3) which has been argued to describe the ground state and low-energy excitations of the Dirac spin liquid phase of quantum antiferromagnets. At finite flavor chemical potential, which corresponds to a Zeeman field perturbing the Dirac spin liquid, we find a “chiral flux” phase which is characterized by the generation of a finite mean emergent gauge flux and, accordingly, the formation of relativistic Landau levels for the Dirac fermions. We use field-theory arguments to argue that in this state a U(1)m magnetic symmetry is spontaneously broken, leading to a gapless photon mode. Because of spin-flux attachment this mode would contribute to the low-energy longitudinal spin response. We numerically compute longitudinal and transverse spin structure factors which match our continuum and lattice mean-field theory predictions. In a different region of the phase diagram, strong fluctuations of the emergent gauge field give rise to an antiferromagnetically ordered state with gapped Dirac fermions coexisting with a deconfined gauge field. We also find an interesting intermediate phase where the chiral flux phase and the antiferromagnetic phase coexist. We argue that our results pave the way to testable predictions for magnetized Dirac spin liquids in frustrated quantum antiferromagnets.

I Introduction

I.1 Motivation

The emergence of nontrivial quantum field theories in condensed matter systems is a remarkable phenomenon. Among the most interesting are strongly interacting gapless field theories with enhanced (generalized) symmetries. Three-dimensional (two space plus one time) quantum electrodynamics, or QED3, is a striking example of such a field theory. Composed of NN two-component Dirac spinors interacting with a U(1) gauge field, QED3 is known to realize a conformal field theory (CFT) for sufficiently large NN (it is commonly believed that N≥4N\geq 4 is sufficient while we caution that distinguishing genuine conformal behavior and pseudocriticality in numerical simulations is challenging) [1, 2, 3, 4]. This CFT contains a rich collection of scaling operators including fermion bilinears (SU(NN) flavor currents and mass terms) and monopole operators, which generate U(1) magnetic fluxes, and which carry nontrivial representations of flavor. As a relatively simple strongly interacting gauge and conformal field theory, QED3 is a test case for nonperturbative methods in the high-energy community. In condensed matter, QED3 has been argued to arise as a ground state of certain quantum antiferromagnets, and in this context is known as a Dirac spin liquid (DSL) [5, 6, 7]. In the DSL, the U(1) gauge field and fermions are emergent: the microscopic formulation begins at a lattice level with only a spin-1/2 direct product Hilbert space. The appearance of QED3 in such a situation is striking and fascinating, worthy of detailed study and verification.

In our opinion, the existence of QED3 as a stable phase of matter (i.e. robust to symmetry-allowed perturbations) is well established in some circumstances (this presupposes that a UV symmetry-allowed SO(6) rank-2 symmetric tensor operator is irrelevant; recent conformal-bootstrap studies have analyzed N=4N=4 QED3 under spectral assumptions concerning this operator [4, 8], but do not by themselves establish its irrelevance). From the field-theory perspective, basic properties of QED3 are understood, e.g. the set of primary fields, rough determinations of their scaling dimensions [3, 9, 4, 8], and how microscopic (UV) symmetries are implemented [10, 11], allowing for a symmetry-based analysis of perturbations [12, 13, 14]. However, more detailed properties such as the computation of multi-point correlation functions, and renormalization group flows under various perturbations, are as yet unknown.

From the condensed matter side, the DSLs have been proposed and investigated in spin-1/2 Heisenberg models on kagomé [15, 7, 16, 17, 18] and triangular [19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 11, 26] lattices by a variety of analytical and numerical techniques. Yet, the understanding of their physical response functions remains limited [27, 28, 29, 30].

In this paper, we extend the understanding of QED3 and the DSL by exploring the effect of a particularly important physical perturbation: an external magnetic field in the condensed matter realization, which couples to the spins via Zeeman interaction. From the QED3 perspective, this field appears as a flavor chemical potential. In experiments on quantum magnets, the study of the phase diagram enriched by the field axis is a routine and powerful way to probe the physics. In QED3, we will see that the flavor chemical potential enjoys an intriguing interplay with the emergent flux, and may, for the DSL, make the emergent structure of the system more apparent. In order to decouple the complicated physics of magnetic monopoles from that of the emergent orbital flux and relativistic Landau levels of fractionalized spinons, which is the focus of our study, we propose to investigate a “mixed” lattice gauge theory that suppresses magnetic monopole events when one takes the continuum limit along the temporal direction. We stress that within this mixed theory, a magnetic flux through spatial plaquette remains well defined. All our simulations reported below adhere to this central idea. Our simulations therefore isolate the field-induced flux physics in a controlled setting, establishing the chiral flux (CF) phase and its characteristic signatures in the dynamical spin response within the mixed theory while disentangling them from the additional effects of dynamical monopoles. How these monopole effects reshape the resulting phase in a fully compact gauge theory, as is relevant to microscopic spin models, remains an important question for future work.

Our investigation is inspired by work of Ran et al. [31] who considered the response to a Zeeman field in a DSL on a kagomé lattice, using a parton mean-field approach and a variational wave function. It is also related to recent work discussing spontaneous symmetry breaking in QED3 in zero field for N=2N=2, for which there is believed not to be a stable CFT [32]. Yet at the same time, recent lattice model quantum Monte Carlo simulations of QED3 have shown signatures of DSL and its phase transitions to confined phases at the spatial scale of 20×2020\times 20 [33, 34, 35].

I.2 Model

Here we carry out a numerically exact determinant quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) study of a lattice model for QED3 derived from the one in Refs. [33, 34] on a cubic space-time lattice (square spatial lattice). The model is defined by the action

S\displaystyle S =∑i,n[ψi†(τn)(ψi(τn)−ψi(τn−1))\displaystyle=\sum_{i,n}\left[\psi^{\dagger}_{i}(\tau_{n})(\psi_{i}(\tau_{n})-\psi_{i}(\tau_{n-1}))\right.
−12Bψi†(τn)σzψi(τn)]\displaystyle\left.-\frac{1}{2}B\psi^{\dagger}_{i}(\tau_{n})\sigma^{z}\psi_{i}(\tau_{n})\right]
−t∑⟨i​j⟩,n[ei​ai​j​(τn)ψi†(τn)ψj(τn)+h.c.]\displaystyle-t\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,n}\left[e^{ia_{ij}(\tau_{n})}\psi^{\dagger}_{i}(\tau_{n})\psi_{j}(\tau_{n})+\textrm{h.c.}\right]
+1J∑⟨i​j⟩,n[ai​j(τn)−ai​j(τn−1)]2\displaystyle+\frac{1}{J}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,n}\left[a_{ij}(\tau_{n})-a_{ij}(\tau_{n-1})\right]^{2} (1)

where ψi=(ψi,↑ψi,↓)\psi_{i}=\begin{pmatrix}\psi_{i,\uparrow}\\ \psi_{i,\downarrow}\end{pmatrix} is a fermionic spinor, ai​ja_{ij} is a bosonic scalar and it acts as a U(1) gauge field, i,j∈[1,L2]i,j\in[1,L^{2}] labels sites of the square lattice, and ⟨i​j⟩\langle ij\rangle is the nearest neighbor bond, with the simulated spatial system size L=6,8,10,⋯,20L=6,8,10,\cdots,20. The temporal system size is Nτ=1T​Δ​τ=20​LN_{\tau}=\frac{1}{T\Delta\tau}=20L, where τn∈[0,β=1T=2L]\tau_{n}\in[0,\beta=\frac{1}{T}=2L] labels the discrete imaginary time with step Δ​τ=0.1\Delta\tau=0.1 in our setting and n∈[0,Nτ]n\in[0,N_{\tau}] is its integer index, as shown Fig. 1 (a). The partition function Z=Tr​{e−S}Z={\rm Tr}\,\{e^{-S}\} is obtained by tracing out all fermion and boson degrees of freedom, see Eq. (2).

The model in Eq. (1) is a somewhat unconventional variant of the gauge theory. In particular, while the fermion terms are fully periodic under a 2​π2\pi shift of ai​j​(τn)a_{ij}(\tau_{n}) on any single bond at any single imaginary time τn\tau_{n}, the “Maxwell” term in the last line of Eq. (1) lacks this periodicity. Thus the action lacks such periodicity and instead has a subsystem periodicity: it is invariant under the shift ai​j​(τn)→ai​j​(τn)+2​π​mi​ja_{ij}(\tau_{n})\rightarrow a_{ij}(\tau_{n})+2\pi m_{ij} with any set of integers mi​jm_{ij} which are time independent. This choice was made in order to be as close as possible to the noncompact theory (which lacks any periodicity) while still allowing the model to dynamically choose a nontrivial flux through spatial slices (horizontal surfaces in space-time defined by τn=const.\tau_{n}=\mathrm{const}.). We refer to our model as the “mixed” compact-noncompact theory, or simply the “mixed” theory.

It is well known that the compact (fully periodic) theory includes “magnetic monopoles”: pointlike defects in spacetime (instantons) associated with nonzero quantized values of magnetic three-flux integrated over a closed space-time surface. These defects are dynamical degrees of freedom and to be summed over in a partition function for a fully compact U(1) gauge theory. The critical phases of QED3 can suffer instabilities driven by monopole proliferation. When exactly such instability occurs depends upon the phase in question and subtle lattice physics due to Berry phase effects [10]. Our simulation has been tailored to suppress monopoles in order to evade such instabilities.

The behavior of monopoles in the mixed theory is somewhat subtle. As we show explicitly in an analytically tractable model in Supplemental Material (SM) [36], the theory Eq. (1) still admits monopole excitations owing to the periodic (in ai​ja_{ij}) fermion-gauge coupling, albeit with a highly constrained mobility (i.e. quantized magnetic flux can only penetrate surfaces perpendicular to the temporal direction). As a result, taking the continuum limit along the temporal direction suppresses these monopole excitations, so that the mixed theory behaves as a noncompact gauge theory, except that the net flux through a full spatial slice is free and energetically chosen by the model. Our numerical simulations are carried out well into this limit, which corresponds to a highly anisotropic space-time lattice (with Nτ≫NN_{\tau}\gg N). Therefore in our simulation we expect stable phases with both free and strongly interacting photons. We remark that, even when monopoles are suppressed, one may consider monopole operators as nondynamical “insertions” defined by modifying the partition function appropriately.

Our analysis of the DQMC results rests on an understanding of the symmetries of the problem. In this paper, we follow modern conventions and only refer to symmetries of those operations which act nontrivially on physical states, i.e., on gauge-invariant observables. In particular, gauge invariance does not qualify as a symmetry, but rather reflects a constraint on the Hilbert space. We list important physical symmetries of the lattice model (1) which are relevant to our analysis:

  1. 1.

    Considering the model with nn flavors of fermions (with flavor index α=1​…​n\alpha=1\ldots n), in zero applied Zeeman field B=0B=0, there is an SU(nn) flavor symmetry, which we denote SU(nn)f. Here we focus on n=2n=2. This symmetry is lowered upon application of a finite Zeeman field B≠0B\neq 0 (explicitly breaking SU(2)f symmetry) to U(1)f, associated with rotations around the field axis in flavor space, which acts on Dirac fermions as U​(1)f:ψi​(τn)→e−i​α​σz​ψi​(τn)\mathrm{U(1)}_{f}:\psi_{i}(\tau_{n})\to e^{-i\alpha\sigma^{z}}\psi_{i}(\tau_{n}) with α∈[0,2​π)\alpha\in[0,2\pi) and leaves the U(1) gauge field invariant.

  2. 2.

    In the time-continuum limit, as discussed above, there is a conserved magnetic flux through the spatial slices of the lattice. This may be written Φ⁡(τn)=∑(rx,ry)mod​((∇×a)(rx,ry,τn),2​π)\Phi(\tau_{n})=\sum_{(r_{x},r_{y})}\textrm{mod}((\nabla\times a)_{(r_{x},r_{y},\tau_{n})},2\pi) and the conservation means that Φ⁡(τn)\Phi(\tau_{n}) is independent of τn\tau_{n} for finite-action configurations in the Monte Carlo procedure in the continuum time limit. This conserved flux defines a U(1)m “magnetic” symmetry on quantum states, i.e. the conserved flux is the symmetry generator for the U(1)m symmetry. The definition of the symmetry generator is the way a symmetry is defined in quantum mechanics. In a phase in which fermions are gapped, this symmetry can be made manifest through an explicit duality transformation of the mixed theory, which is presented in Supplemental Material [36]. This reveals that the spontaneous breaking of this symmetry manifests in a linearly dispersing “dual” Goldstone mode, i.e. a photon.

  3. 3.

    There is a discrete time-reversal invariance 𝒯\mathcal{T} (ψi​(τ)→ψi†​(−τ)\psi_{i}(\tau)\rightarrow\psi^{\dagger}_{i}(-\tau), ψi†​(τ)→−ψi​(−τ)\psi^{\dagger}_{i}(\tau)\rightarrow-\psi_{i}(-\tau), ai​j​(τ)→−ai​j​(−τ)a_{ij}(\tau)\rightarrow-a_{ij}(-\tau)) which is a symmetry of Eq. (1) also at finite Zeeman fields B≠0B\neq 0. Hence, 𝒯\mathcal{T} is distinct from the usual time-reversal symmetry for spin-1/2 particles, the latter being broken explicitly by finite Zeeman fields B≠0B\neq 0.

  4. 4.

    The model further enjoys spatial translation symmetries (along with point group symmetries, which are not of immediate relevance for the remainder of our work). Translations along x^\hat{x} act as Tx:ψi​(τ)→ψTx​(i)​(τ)T_{x}:\psi_{i}(\tau)\to\psi_{T_{x}(i)}(\tau) and ai​j​(τn)→aTx​(i),Tx​(j)​(τn)a_{ij}(\tau_{n})\to a_{T_{x}(i),T_{x}(j)}(\tau_{n}) with Tx​(i)≡i+x^T_{x}(i)\equiv i+\hat{x}, and analogously for TyT_{y}.

We summarize the key aspects of the “mixed” gauge theory, and in particular the consequence of the non-periodicity in ai​ja_{ij} of the time-derivative Maxwell term. For nonzero Trotterization, monopoles are allowed, but they are very strongly suppressed with diminishing time discretization, and become fully absent in the time-continuum limit. In this limit, a perfectly conserved magnetic flux Φ\Phi defines a U​(1)mU(1)_{m} symmetry.

We emphasize that the lattice model of Eq. (1) is a form of QED3 in that it describes fermions interacting with a bosonic U(1) gauge field, but it is not a continuum model. Standard continuum QED3 contains NN species of two-component Dirac fermions coupled to such a gauge field. In a certain regime such a theory arises as a continuum limit of Eq. (1) (see below). Because of fermion doubling, the low energy continuum theory has N=2​nN=2n Dirac fermions and the SU(nn)f lattice symmetry is enlarged to an emergent SU(NN)f = SU(2​n2n) = SU(4)f symmetry. However, we should keep in mind that residual effects originating from lattice corrections to the continuum limit preserve only the SU(2)f subgroup. Accordingly, we focus on the robust exact symmetries of the lattice model to characterize the system.

I.3 Summary of results

Aided by these symmetries, our DQMC results, obtained on finite systems of dimensions β×L×L\beta\times L\times L, as explained above, are summarized in the low-temperature phase diagram of Fig. 1 (b), spanned by the axes of gauge fluctuation J/tJ/t and magnetic field B/tB/t. To characterize the symmetries and their breaking, we introduce order parameters. There are two manifest order parameters: N+=(−1)i​⟨ψi†​σ+​ψi⟩N^{+}=(-1)^{i}\langle\psi^{\dagger}_{i}\sigma^{+}\psi_{i}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\rangle, which describes spontaneous breaking of the U(1)f flavor symmetry to form antiferromagnetic (AFM) spin order in the XY plane, and χ=⟨sin⁡Φ□⟩\chi=\langle\sin\Phi_{\Box}\rangle, a chirality, which describes broken 𝒯\mathcal{T} symmetry. Here Φ□=∇×a\Phi_{\Box}=\nabla\times a is the flux through a spatial plaquette, given by the lattice curl of the gauge field. A third order parameter, which is hidden, characterizes the U(1)m magnetic symmetry: this is a monopole operator ℳ+\mathcal{M}^{+}, which creates a 2​π2\pi flux in the gauge field. We do not currently measure ℳ+\mathcal{M}^{+} in our simulations, but its presence can be deduced from an understanding of the corresponding Goldstone mode: the Goldstone mode of the U(1)m symmetry is the photon of the gauge field.

We observe three manifestly symmetry-broken phases as visible in the phase diagram Fig. 1: an antiferromagnetic phase, in which N+N^{+} is nonzero but χ=0\chi=0, a chiral flux phase in which χ≠0\chi\neq 0 but N+=0N^{+}=0, and an overlapping chiral AFM phase in which both N+N^{+} and χ\chi are nonzero. We also find two symmetric phases: a Dirac spin liquid phase and a polarized phase at strong field in which the spins are nearly fully aligned with the field (full polarization is not possible at finite temperatures where our simulations are done). In all the phases except the DSL, the U(1)m symmetry is spontaneously broken, i.e. ℳ+≠0\mathcal{M}^{+}\neq 0, witnessed by the presence of a linearly dispersing free-photon mode. We provide an overview of various phases of the model and the symmetries that they preserve and/or spontaneously break in Table 1.

In addition to the phase diagram, we explore the magnetic spectra of the gauge-invariant fermion bilinears – the spin operators in the condensed matter language – of QED3. Universal features of these spectra provide signatures of fractionalization and emergent gauge fields in quantum magnets proximate to a DSL phase. We are particularly interested in uncovering structures that are unexpected without spin liquid physics, and which might be striking aspects to seek experimentally. In that regard, we focus particularly on the chiral phase in which the emergence of Landau-Hofstadter bands that result from the fractional flux in the gauge field may be reflected in the spin correlations. We present DQMC results for the longitudinal and transverse dynamical spin susceptibilities, and demonstrate a strong correlation between these correlations and a mean-field result which precisely describes fermions in Hofstadter bands. We observe a clear splitting of spectral weight into multiple features that can be understood from the effective enlargement of the magnetic unit cell of fermions experiencing a fractional flux per plaquette, despite the lack of translational symmetry breaking in the system. In some cases features reminiscent of the Landau-level nature of spinon bands are visible in the numerically obtained magnetic spectra. Our DQMC results for the longitudinal spin structure factor further show signatures of a gapless mode as the possible manifestation of the gapless photon, originating from gauge field fluctuations and therefore a manifestly beyond-mean-field result.

I.4 Guide to the paper

The paper is organized as follows: Sec. II lays out the lattice implementation of the mixed QED3 model and its DQMC numerical algorithm (Sec. II.1), and we further explain the Monte Carlo update scheme of the gauge field to overcome its slow dynamics and anisotropic space-time gauge choice (Sec. II.2). Sec. II.3, on the other hand, provides the theoretical discussion of the different phases (DSL, CF, AFM) in the phase diagram at the continuum limit with random phase approximation (RPA). Section III presents the phase diagram. Section III.1 provides the lattice mean-field analysis at J=0J=0, while Sec. III.2 determines the phase boundaries using DQMC simulations at finite JJ and BB. Sec. IV focuses on the data and analysis of the magnetic spectra in the CF and AFM states, starting from the field-theoretical calculation (Sec. IV.1), the lattice mean-field calculation (Sec. IV.2) and more importantly, to the DQMC simulation results and the discussion of similarity and difference between the numerically unbiased solution and the mean-field analysis (Sec. IV.3). Sec. V provides the discussions of the results and makes connection with potential DSL and CF phases in frustrated magnets and their experimental detections.

Sections I and II of the Supplemental Material (SM) [36] describe the magnetic spectra calculated using lattice mean-field and low-energy field-theory approaches, respectively. Section III reviews Larmor’s theorem and its application to the magnetic spectra at the Γ\Gamma point. Section IV presents flux-correlation results for the pure gauge theory and for the DSL and AFM phases. Section V explains the zz-direction flux insertion and global update scheme used in the DQMC simulations. Section VI discusses the U(1)m symmetry and the duality map. Section VII compares the mean-field and DQMC magnetic spectra at B/t=2B/t=2. Section VIII presents a finite-size analysis of the order parameters.

II Methods and Theoretical Expectations

II.1 QED3\text{QED}_{3} with lattice DQMC

As mentioned in Sec. I, we consider the QED3 theory on the cubic lattice, with the action in Eq. (1). The mixed nature of the gauge coupling penalizes monopoles more than in a compact gauge theory, and indeed they are parametrically suppressed in the temporal continuum limit. In that regime we expect our mixed gauge theory to act like a noncompact gauge theory. We discard the KK term used in prior work (Ref. [33]), because it adds an undesirable additional pinning field favoring π\pi-flux in the gauge field, masking the emergence of non-π\pi-flux states with nonzero Zeeman field.

In the DQMC study of the action above, the partition function takes the form

Z=∫D⁡(a,ψ¯,ψ)​e−(Sa+Sf)=∫D​a​e−Sa​Trψ​[e−Sf],\displaystyle Z=\int D(a,\bar{\psi},\psi)\ e^{-\left(S_{a}+S_{f}\right)}=\int Da\ e^{-S_{a}}\operatorname{Tr}_{\psi}\left[e^{-S_{f}}\right], (2)

where SaS_{a} is the pure gauge field action (the last line in Eq. (1)) and SfS_{f} contains all the remaining contributions which are quadratic in fermions. The gauge field ai​ja_{ij} is an unconstrained continuous variable living on the nearest spatial bonds of cubic lattice as shown in Fig. 1 (a). The quadratic fermion ψi\psi_{i} can be traced out to give

Trψ⁡[e−Sf]=\displaystyle\operatorname{Tr}_{\psi}\left[e^{-S_{f}}\right]= ∏α[det⁡(𝐈+∏n=1Nτ𝐁τn,α)]\displaystyle\prod_{\alpha}\left[\operatorname{det}\left(\mathbf{I}+\prod_{n=1}^{N_{\tau}}\mathbf{B}_{\tau_{n},\alpha}\right)\right]

𝐌α=(𝟏00⋯0𝐁τNτ,α−𝐁τ1,α𝟏0⋯000−𝐁τ2,α𝟏⋯00⋱000⋯𝟏0000⋯−𝐁τNτ−1,α𝟏)\mathbf{M}_{\alpha}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{1}&0&0&\cdots&0&\mathbf{B}_{\tau_{N_{\tau}},\alpha}\\ -\mathbf{B}_{\tau_{1},\alpha}&\mathbf{1}&0&\cdots&0&0\\ 0&-\mathbf{B}_{\tau_{2},\alpha}&\mathbf{1}&\cdots&0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\cdots&\mathbf{1}&0\\ 0&0&0&\cdots&-\mathbf{B}_{\tau_{N_{\tau}-1},\alpha}&\mathbf{1}\end{pmatrix}

For the case without Zeeman field, it can be shown that det⁡𝐌α∈ℝ\operatorname{det}\mathbf{M}_{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R} and det⁡𝐌↑=det⁡𝐌↓\operatorname{det}\mathbf{M}_{\uparrow}=\operatorname{det}\mathbf{M}_{\downarrow}, thus sign-problem-free for Monte Carlo simulation [33, 38]. With nonzero Zeeman field, det⁡𝐌α\operatorname{det}\mathbf{M}_{\alpha} is complex. Thus the partition function Eq. (2) is amenable to DQMC method [39, 40, 41].

II.2 Update scheme in DQMC simulations

In a nonzero Zeeman field B>0B>0, the preferred configurations of the gauge field have a flux Φ□\Phi_{\Box} different from π\pi per plaquette at the mean field level [7]. Beyond mean field, the flux on each plaquette remains a gauge-invariant observable and the energy of the system depends on the flux configuration. We expect in the DQMC simulation, the probability distribution of the flux will thus generally deviate from one centered at π\pi. Therefore, a Monte Carlo update method that changes the flux directly would be highly desirable from the perspective of efficiency. To this end, we combine a local update of the gauge field on each bond ai​j​(τn)→ai​j​(τn)+δ​aa_{ij}(\tau_{n})\rightarrow a_{ij}(\tau_{n})+\delta a with a global update that can change the flux directly in the entire lattice.

To perform the space-time global update, based on the zz-direction flux insertion technique [42, 43], one can update the gauge field ai​j​(τn)a_{ij}(\tau_{n}) for all spatial bonds and imaginary time layers simultaneously with the following scheme,

ai​j​(τn)→ai​j​(τn)+ao,i​ja_{ij}(\tau_{n})\rightarrow a_{ij}(\tau_{n})+a_{o,ij} (4)

with ao,i​ja_{o,ij} the introduced extra orbital field. In the Landau gauge, ao,i​ja_{o,ij} for bonds in the xx direction is −2​π​y​NΦL2-\frac{2\pi yN_{\Phi}}{L^{2}}. While for bonds in the yy direction, depending on the location, ao,i​j=0a_{o,ij}=0 for bonds away from boundary and ao,i​j=2​π​x​NΦLa_{o,ij}=\frac{2\pi xN_{\Phi}}{L} for those cross boundary in yy direction. x,yx,y in the expression is the position of the bond in unit of lattice constant and NΦN_{\Phi} is an integer. For detailed derivation of the Landau gauge on the lattice with zz-direction flux insertion, please refer to Sec. V of the SM [36].

At each global update, NΦN_{\Phi} is randomly chosen and we apply the same ao,i​ja_{o,ij} (according to the random NΦN_{\Phi} and the Landau gauge) for all imaginary time layers. If the update is accepted, a uniform flux 2​π​NΦL2\frac{2\pi N_{\Phi}}{L^{2}} is inserted into the model. In DQMC simulations, such an update requires the computation of determinant in Eq. (3) from scratch and it is expensive. We thus choose to perform a combination of a sweep of Metropolis local updates plus 44 times of such global updates, which is defined as one complete sweep in DQMC simulation. In this way, the number of global updates does not scale with system size. As mentioned above, global update helps to quickly evolve to the desired flux sector and local update will explore the whole phase space ergodically.

II.3 Continuum limit and random phase approximation

To provide a framework to understand the numerical results, we discuss the continuum limit of Eq. (1) and analyze it in the random phase approximation (RPA), allowing for the possibility of spontaneous AFM order. To obtain the continuum limit, we assume first small Zeeman field B≪1B\ll 1, so that the flux Φ□≈π\Phi_{\Box}\approx\pi. We then take ai,i+μ​(τn)=a¯i,i+μ+Aμ​(xi,yi,τn)a_{i,i+\mu}(\tau_{n})=\bar{a}_{i,i+\mu}+A_{\mu}(x_{i},y_{i},\tau_{n}), where μ=x,y\mu=x,y and a¯i,i+μ\bar{a}_{i,i+\mu} is a c-number background gauge field representing the π\pi flux, ∇×a¯=π\nabla\times\bar{a}=\pi, and Aμ​(x,y,τ)A_{\mu}(x,y,\tau) is a slowly varying continuum field describing small deviations from π\pi flux. When J≲1J\lesssim 1, we may assume the fluctuations of AμA_{\mu} are weak, and that the fermionic action may be approximated by the low energy form near zero frequency and the zero energy Dirac points of the π\pi flux problem.

For concreteness, we take the gauge a¯i,i+x=0\bar{a}_{i,i+x}=0 and a¯i,i+y=π​xi\bar{a}_{i,i+y}=\pi x_{i}, which makes the hopping on the yy-oriented bonds with odd xix_{i} to be negative relative to other hoppings. This choice doubles the unit cell along the xx-direction. Then the lattice fermion ψi,σ\psi_{i,\sigma} (with σ\sigma a spin index) can be decomposed into slow-varying continuum fields Ψs,v,σ​(x,y,τ)\Psi_{s,v,\sigma}(x,y,\tau) with s=mod​(xi,2)=0,1s=\textrm{mod}(x_{i},2)=0,1 a sublattice index, v=0,1v=0,1 a valley index, as follows:

ψi,σ​(τn)∼\displaystyle\psi_{i,\sigma}(\tau_{n})\sim ∑v=0,1(i​(−1)v)xi+yi​Ψmod​(xi,2),v,σ​(xi,yi,τn),\displaystyle\sum_{v=0,1}(i(-1)^{v})^{x_{i}+y_{i}}\Psi_{\textrm{mod}(x_{i},2),v,\sigma}(x_{i},y_{i},\tau_{n}),
ψi,σ†​(τn)∼\displaystyle\psi^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}(\tau_{n})\sim ∑v=0,1(−i​(−1)v)xi+yi​Ψmod​(xi,2),v,σ†​(xi,yi,τn).\displaystyle\sum_{v=0,1}(-i(-1)^{v})^{x_{i}+y_{i}}\Psi^{\dagger}_{\textrm{mod}(x_{i},2),v,\sigma}(x_{i},y_{i},\tau_{n}). (5)

We insert this into the action and gradient expand assuming slow variations of AμA_{\mu} and Ψ\Psi, so that the spatial part of the fermion action [the hopping term in Eq. (1)] turns into the sum of two valley contributions ∝−it(−1)v∫dτd2xΨs,v,σ†(τs,s′x∂x+τs,s′z∂y)Ψs′,v,σ\propto-it(-1)^{v}\int d\tau d^{2}x\,\Psi^{\dagger}_{s,v,\sigma}(\tau^{x}_{s,s^{\prime}}\partial_{x}+\tau^{z}_{s,s^{\prime}}\partial_{y})\Psi_{s^{\prime},v,\sigma}. This is followed by the transformations Ψs,1,σ→τs​s′y​Ψs′,1,σ\Psi_{s,1,\sigma}\rightarrow\tau^{y}_{ss^{\prime}}\Psi_{s^{\prime},1,\sigma}, Ψs,0,σ†→Ψ¯s′,0,σ​τs′​sy\Psi^{\dagger}_{s,0,\sigma}\rightarrow\bar{\Psi}_{s^{\prime},0,\sigma}\tau^{y}_{s^{\prime}s}, which are not unitary but allowed since Ψ¯\bar{\Psi} and Ψ\Psi are independent in the path integral, and the “renaming” of the Grassman integration field in the valley v=1v=1 as Ψs,1,σ†→Ψ¯s,1,σ\Psi_{s,1,\sigma}^{\dagger}\to\bar{\Psi}_{s,1,\sigma}. The result is the continuum action S=∫d​τ​d2​x​ℒS=\int\!d\tau d^{2}x\,\mathcal{L}, with

ℒ=∑μ=02\displaystyle\mathcal{L}=\sum_{\mu=0}^{2} Ψ¯γμvμ(∂μ+iAμ)Ψ−b2Ψ¯γ0σzΨ\displaystyle\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{\mu}v_{\mu}(\partial_{\mu}+iA_{\mu})\Psi-\frac{b}{2}\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{0}\sigma^{z}\Psi
+1g∑μ=x,y(∂τAμ)2,\displaystyle+\frac{1}{g}\sum_{\mu=x,y}(\partial_{\tau}A_{\mu})^{2}, (6)

where v0=1v_{0}=1, v1=v2≡v=2​t/Δ​τv_{1}=v_{2}\equiv v=2t/\Delta\tau, b=B/Δ​τb=B/\Delta\tau, and g=J/Δ​τg=J/\Delta\tau. We can let γ0=τy\gamma^{0}=\tau^{y}, γ1=τz\gamma^{1}=\tau^{z}, γ2=−τx\gamma^{2}=-\tau^{x}, where the Pauli matrices 𝝉\bm{\tau} are defined to act in the sublattice space, 𝝈\bm{\sigma} acts in the spin space, and we suppressed all the sublattice, valley, and spin indices.

Eq. (6) describes a continuum Dirac theory with 2×2=42\times 2=4 flavors arising from the spin and valley, coupled to the continuum U(1) gauge field AμA_{\mu}, which is precisely QED3 with the gauge choice Aτ=A0=0A_{\tau}=A_{0}=0.

Using the same transformations, we can also obtain the Néel order parameter

N+=ψi†​σ+​ψi​(−1)xi+yi∼Ψ¯​σ+​μx​Ψ,\displaystyle N^{+}=\psi_{i}^{\dagger}\sigma^{+}\psi^{\vphantom{\dagger}}_{i}(-1)^{x_{i}+y_{i}}\sim\bar{\Psi}\sigma^{+}\mu^{x}\Psi, (7)

where σ+=(σx+i​σy)/2\sigma^{+}=(\sigma^{x}+i\sigma^{y})/2 and we introduced the 𝝁\bm{\mu} Pauli matrices acting in the valley space.

Such continuum theory is capable of describing the quantum phases close to the zero field DSL, which includes the DSL itself, the CF phase, and the AFM. We discuss each in turn, with an eye to the predictions for various correlation functions and spectral properties to be tested in the DQMC simulations in Secs. III and IV.

II.3.1 DSL

The DSL occurs for b=0b=0, in which case this is precisely noncompact QED3 without any applied potential. This has been analyzed extensively and is believed to describe a scale-invariant conformal field theory. Consequently, power law behavior is expected for all gauge-invariant observables. Because of fermion doubling in DSL phase, the CFT is expected to have emergent SU(4) (∼SO⁡(6)\sim\mathrm{SO}(6) up to a sign) symmetry, which enlarges the microscopic SU(2) spin symmetry and some discrete operations in the space group. In the CFT of SU(4) QED3, the set of primary fields with low scaling dimensions are as follows:

  • •

    the set of SU(4) conserved currents Jμa=Ψ¯​γμ​𝖳a​ΨJ_{\mu}^{a}=\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{\mu}\mathsf{T}^{a}\Psi, where μ\mu is a space-time index and aa ranges over the 15 generators 𝖳a\mathsf{T}^{a} of SU(4). Like all conserved currents in a (2+1)(2+1)-dimensional CFT, the currents have the exact scaling dimension ΔJ=2\Delta_{J}=2.

  • •

    fermion bilinears or mass terms: a singlet Ms=Ψ¯​ΨM_{s}=\bar{\Psi}\Psi and a set of adjoints Ma=Ψ¯​𝖳a​ΨM_{a}=\bar{\Psi}\mathsf{T}_{a}\Psi, where a=1​…​15a=1\ldots 15 range over the SU(4) generators. A priori, these two sets have independent scaling dimensions, Δs\Delta_{s} and Δadj\Delta_{\rm adj}, respectively. An estimate from Ref. [3] is Δs≈2.3\Delta_{s}\approx 2.3, Δadj∈(1.4,1.7)\Delta_{\rm adj}\in(1.4,1.7).

  • •

    a set of 6 monopole operators ℳq\mathcal{M}_{q} (and their conjugates ℳq†\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}_{q}), which form an antisymmetric tensor representation of SU(4), or a real vector representation of SO(6), hence q=1,…,6q=1,\ldots,6. The estimated scaling dimension from the large NfN_{f} expansion [9] is ΔM≈1.0\Delta_{M}\approx 1.0.

These scaling operators and their composites (products) and descendants (derivatives) appear in the long-distance correlations of lattice quantities. For example, we expect that the DSL should exhibit flux-flux correlations dictated by ΔJ=2\Delta_{J}=2, which implies that, for example, the long-time correlations of the local flux should behave as ⟨Φ□​(τ)​Φ□​(0)⟩∼τ−4\langle\Phi_{\Box}(\tau)\Phi_{\Box}(0)\rangle\sim\tau^{-4}. Note that this is different from the result in nonconformal phases described below in which the flux correlations arise from the Goldstone mode of spontaneously broken U(1)m symmetry, and correspond to that of a free-photon theory with ⟨Φ□​(τ)​Φ□​(0)⟩∼τ−3\langle\Phi_{\Box}(\tau)\Phi_{\Box}(0)\rangle\sim\tau^{-3} (our numerical results for these temporal flux correlation functions are discussed in Sec. IV of the SM [36]).

The spin correlations, i.e., the dynamic structure factor, in the DSL probe CFT operators, which can appear in the continuum limit of individual spin operators. In this noncompact theory, the spin operators (like all operators we consider) conserve flux, and hence monopoles cannot appear in their expansion. Rather, the fermion bilinears Ma>0M_{a>0} are expected to dominate. One of these operators (see below in the discussion of the AFM phase) corresponds to the Néel field, so that the staggered spin correlations should show power-law behavior with a decay exponent 2​Δa​d​j∈(2.8,3.5)2\Delta_{adj}\in(2.8,3.5). Our DQMC results indeed reveal the consistent power-law behavior in spin correlation with 2​Δ=3.2​(1)2\Delta=3.2(1), as shown in Fig. 10 (b) below. In fact, previous QMC simulation for finite sizes of 20×2020\times 20 have found similar power-law decays of the spin and dimer operators, see Fig. 4 in Ref. [33].

It is possible in principle to measure monopole correlations by explicitly including a monopole-antimonopole insertion in the partition function, but we have not done this in the current simulation as it requires a significant technical development. In the DSL phase, this correlation is expected to decay with a power law of 2​ΔM≈22\Delta_{M}\approx 2.

II.3.2 CF phase

In the CF phase, a spontaneous flux ⟨∇×A⟩≠0\langle\nabla\times A\rangle\neq 0 develops. Any nonzero flux causes the Dirac cones to split into Landau levels with energies ϵn=ωc​|n|​sgn⁡(n)\epsilon_{n}=\omega_{c}\sqrt{|n|}\operatorname{sgn}(n), with n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}, and ωc=2​|ϕ|​v\omega_{c}=\sqrt{2|\phi|}v the cyclotron energy when the average flux is ϕ\phi. The latter is determined by the condition that the 0th Landau levels for both valleys are full of up spin fermions and empty of down. This fixes the flux to density relation, ⟨∇×A⟩=ϕ=±π⁡⟨n↑−n↓⟩\langle\nabla\times A\rangle=\phi=\pm\pi\langle n_{\uparrow}-n_{\downarrow}\rangle. Note that a finite flux breaks time-reversal symmetry 𝒯\mathcal{T}, with a spontaneously chosen sign. The Zeeman field accordingly acts as an opposite Fermi level for the two spin polarizations, lying between the 0th and the n=±1n=\pm 1 Landau levels for the up and down spins, respectively. Hence ϵF​α=α​b/2=0.62​α​ωc\epsilon_{F\alpha}=\alpha b/2=0.62\alpha\omega_{c} for α=±1\alpha=\pm 1 corresponding to up and down spins, respectively. This relation between the Zeeman field bb and the spontaneous orbital flux ϕ\phi, and hence ωc\omega_{c}, follows from the mean-field analysis in [31].

We proceed to analyze the effect of this mean-field flux by analyzing the fluctuations of the gauge field and the system’s response. Accordingly, we write Aμ=A¯μ+aμcA_{\mu}=\bar{A}_{\mu}+a^{c}_{\mu}, where ∇×A¯=ϕ\nabla\times\bar{A}=\phi, and aμca^{c}_{\mu} describes the fluctuations of the internal “charge” gauge field. To probe the response, we furthermore add a probe spin gauge field aμsa^{s}_{\mu} which couples to the conserved U(1) spin three-current of the fermions. This field is fictitious but will be used as an infinitesimal source to generate correlation functions and to characterize the spin response. Note that an infinitesimal change of Zeeman field b→b+δ​bb\rightarrow b+\delta b is equivalent to including a small time component of the spin gauge field, a0s=i​δ​ba^{s}_{0}=\mathrm{i}\,\delta b. Observe that a0sa^{s}_{0} couples to the density of up or down spin fermions, α=±1\alpha=\pm 1, with opposite signs.

The full Lagrangian including these fluctuations can therefore be written

ℒ=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}= 1g​(∂τajc)2+∑v=01∑α=±1ℒvDLL​(aμc+α2​aμs,ϵF=α​b2),\displaystyle\frac{1}{g}(\partial_{\tau}a_{j}^{c})^{2}+\sum_{v=0}^{1}\sum_{\alpha=\pm 1}\mathcal{L}_{v}^{\textrm{DLL}}\left(a^{c}_{\mu}+\frac{\alpha}{2}a^{s}_{\mu},\epsilon_{F}=\alpha\frac{b}{2}\right), (8)

where ℒvDLL​(aμ,ϵF)\mathcal{L}_{v}^{\textrm{DLL}}(a_{\mu},\epsilon_{F}) is the Lagrangian for valley vv of Dirac fermion Landau levels coupled to a total gauge field aμa_{\mu} and with Fermi level ϵF\epsilon_{F}.

Now we proceed to carry out an RPA treatment, integrating out the fermions to quadratic order in the gauge fields. Since each spin and valley of fermion is decoupled, their contributions can be added. Each contributes a standard effective action for a system of fully filled and empty Landau levels, consisting of a leading Chern-Simons term whose coefficient is 1/(4​π)1/(4\pi) times the Hall conductivity of those fermions, and a subleading Maxwell term, representing the polarizability of the fermions [44]. The Hall conductivity of each valley of up or down fermion is ±1/2\pm 1/2, capturing the change of Hall conductivity by one unit for occupying or emptying a Landau level, and accounting for particle-hole symmetry.

Consequently, we obtain

ℒeff=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm eff}= ∑α=±1i​α4​π​ϵμ​ν​λ​(aμc+α2​aμs)​∂ν(aλc+α2​aλs)\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha=\pm 1}i\,\frac{\alpha}{4\pi}\epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda}\left(a_{\mu}^{c}+\frac{\alpha}{2}a_{\mu}^{s}\right)\partial_{\nu}\left(a_{\lambda}^{c}+\frac{\alpha}{2}a_{\lambda}^{s}\right)
+1g​(∂τajc)2+12​g~​∑α=±1(fμ​νc+α2​fμ​νs)2,\displaystyle+\frac{1}{g}(\partial_{\tau}a_{j}^{c})^{2}+\frac{1}{2\tilde{g}}\sum_{\alpha=\pm 1}\left(f_{\mu\nu}^{c}+\frac{\alpha}{2}f_{\mu\nu}^{s}\right)^{2}, (9)

where fμ​νσ=∂μaνσ−∂νaμσf_{\mu\nu}^{\sigma}=\partial_{\mu}a_{\nu}^{\sigma}-\partial_{\nu}a_{\mu}^{\sigma}, and the quantized Chern-Simons terms occupy the first line (note that these terms appear with a factor of ii in our Euclidean field theory), and the cutoff dependent and unquantized Maxwell terms the second.

Expanding and regrouping the terms, we find

ℒeff=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm eff}= i​12​π​ϵμ​ν​λ​aμs​∂νaλc+1g′​(fμ​νc)2+14​g~​(fμ​νs)2,\displaystyle\,i\,\frac{1}{2\pi}\epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda}a_{\mu}^{s}\partial_{\nu}a_{\lambda}^{c}+\frac{1}{g^{\prime}}(f_{\mu\nu}^{c})^{2}+\frac{1}{4\tilde{g}}(f_{\mu\nu}^{s})^{2}, (10)

consisting of a mixed Chern-Simons term for spin and charge, and Maxwell contributions, describing renormalization of gauge field charges and velocities that depend on the regularization scheme [45].

Eq. (10) is short but encodes several important conclusions, which we now discuss.

Gapless mode.

First set the probe field as=0a^{s}=0. Then Eq. (10) becomes just a Maxwell term for the fluctuating gauge field. This describes a massless photon, i.e. a single branch of linearly dispersing mode ω=c​|k|\omega=c|k| with cc the speed of “light”. This can be regarded as simply arising from the original gauge field in the lattice model, and is protected by gauge symmetry. We discuss the alternative view as a Goldstone mode of spontaneously broken U(1)m symmetry below.

From this effective action, one can calculate the flux-flux correlations, ⟨Φ□​(τ)​Φ□​(0)⟩∼τ−3\langle\Phi_{\Box}(\tau)\Phi_{\Box}(0)\rangle\sim\tau^{-3}. This behavior, different from the DSL, is characteristic of the Goldstone mode phase. An explicit demonstration of this conclusion on the lattice is given in Sec. IV of the SM [36].

Low energy spectral weight.

The gapless photon also appears in the correlation of SzS^{z} operators. To see this, note that the time component of the probe field, a0sa_{0}^{s} couples to the conserved spin density Sz=12​Ψ¯​γ0​σz​ΨS^{z}=\frac{1}{2}\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{0}\sigma^{z}\Psi. Hence the derivative δ​ℒeff/δ⁡(δ​b)\delta\mathcal{L}_{\rm eff}/\delta(\delta b) gives the representation of the spin operator in the effective free photon theory. This gives Sz∼∇×acS^{z}\sim\nabla\times a^{c}, i.e. the low-energy spin correlations are identical to those of the emergent magnetic flux. Calculating the latter, one obtains

⟨Sz​Sz⟩ω,𝐪∼12​χ​c​q​δ​(ω−c​q),\langle S^{z}S^{z}\rangle_{\omega,{\bf q}}\sim\frac{1}{2}\chi cq\delta(\omega-cq), (11)

for small ω,q\omega,q, where χ=1N​∑i∂⟨Siz⟩/∂B>0\chi=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\partial\langle S_{i}^{z}\rangle/\partial B>0 is the susceptibility. Here we used the compressible nature of the CF phase and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem to determine the prefactor, since χ\chi is given by the limit ω→0\omega\rightarrow 0 followed by q→0q\rightarrow 0 of the longitudinal dynamical susceptibility. We present our DQMC results for the longitudinal susceptibility, and analyze them in this context, in Sec. IV.3.

Monopole condensate.

In the language of generalized symmetry, the gapless photon should be viewed as a Goldstone mode of a spontaneously broken U(1)m symmetry. However, there are two microscopic U(1) symmetries in the model, and only a single Goldstone mode. This means there must remain an unbroken U(1) subgroup of the original U(1)m×{}_{m}\timesU(1)f symmetry. This statement is also seemingly evident from Eq. (8), which is diagonal in spin σ\sigma so still invariant under U(1)f rotations.

To precisely identify the broken symmetry, we would like to write down the corresponding order parameter. Because it should transform under the U(1)m symmetry, it involves an insertion of 2​π2\pi flux, which we associate with a monopole operator ℳ\mathcal{M}. The meaning of ℳp​(τ)\mathcal{M}_{p}(\tau) is that it creates a flux 2​π2\pi through plaquette pp at time τ\tau.

However, the order parameter is not just the “bare” monopole operator ℳ\mathcal{M}. This can be seen from the mixed Chern-Simons term in Eq. (10), which implies that the charge flux ∇×ac\nabla\times a^{c} is tied to the spin density SzS^{z} (conjugate to a0sa^{s}_{0}). Hence, to have a nonzero expectation value, the order parameter must in addition to creating the flux 2​π2\pi also create the associated change in spin Δ​Sz=1\Delta S^{z}=1. Consequently, the order parameter for the broken U(1) symmetry is

ℳord=ℳ​S+,\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ord}}=\mathcal{M}S^{+}, (12)

which combines the insertion of flux with a spin flip. From the above arguments, we expect that

⟨ℳord⟩≠0.\langle\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ord}}\rangle\neq 0. (13)

This operator, as required, breaks U(1)m symmetry but also U(1)f symmetry. This means that the CF state has a hidden breaking of the U(1)f spin-rotation symmetry. Why is it hidden? It is because the order parameter (and hence the state itself) preserves the combination ℳ→ℳ​ei​χ\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}e^{i\chi}, S+→S+​e−i​χS^{+}\rightarrow S^{+}e^{-i\chi}. The latter corresponds to the residual U(1) subgroup in the CF phase. This ensures that the expectation value of any pure spin operator that changes SzS^{z} such as ⟨Si±⟩=0\langle S_{i}^{\pm}\rangle=0 vanishes, and there is no antiferromagnetic order. Only composite observables which involve a change of the flux can detect the breaking of the spin rotation symmetry. Consistent with this observation, the gapless photon does not contribute as an intermediate state in the transverse spin structure factor, which therefore shows a full gap in the CF phase (see also the discussion of gapped transverse susceptibility obtained in our DQMC results as presented in Sec. IV.3).

II.3.3 AFM

In the AFM phase, the average flux is zero, but spontaneous AFM order has developed. While the AFM order arises from Eq. (6) by the effect of gauge fluctuations, we can model it phenomenologically by introducing an AFM order parameter N+​(x,y,τ)N^{+}(x,y,\tau), which weakly fluctuates and couples to the Dirac fermions. Since the system is ordered, it is sufficient to assume N+=|N|​ei​θ​(x,y,τ)N^{+}=|N|e^{i\theta(x,y,\tau)}. The effective Lagrangian in Eq. (6) is then replaced by

ℒ=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}= ∑μ=02Ψ¯γμvμ(∂μ+iAμ)Ψ−b2Ψ¯γ0σzΨ\displaystyle\sum_{\mu=0}^{2}\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{\mu}v_{\mu}(\partial_{\mu}+iA_{\mu})\Psi-\frac{b}{2}\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{0}\sigma^{z}\Psi
−|N|(ei​θ​Ψ¯​σ−​μx​Ψ+h.c.)+1g​∑μ=x,y(∂τAμ)2.\displaystyle-|N|\left(e^{i\theta}\bar{\Psi}\sigma^{-}\mu^{x}\Psi+\textrm{h.c.}\right)+\frac{1}{g}\sum_{\mu=x,y}(\partial_{\tau}A_{\mu})^{2}. (14)

Now we make the unitary transformation Ψ→ei​θ​σz/2​Ψ\Psi\rightarrow e^{i\theta\sigma^{z}/2}\Psi, Ψ¯→Ψ¯e−iθσz/2\bar{\Psi}\rightarrow\bar{\Psi}e^{-i\theta\sigma^{z}/2}, which is chosen to remove the dependence of the action on a constant phase θ\theta. When this phase depends upon space and time, the result is

ℒ\displaystyle\mathcal{L} →∑μ=02Ψ¯γμvμ(∂μ+iAμ+i2∂μθσz)Ψ−b2Ψ¯γ0σzΨ\displaystyle\rightarrow\sum_{\mu=0}^{2}\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{\mu}v_{\mu}(\partial_{\mu}+iA_{\mu}+\frac{i}{2}\partial_{\mu}\theta\sigma^{z})\Psi-\frac{b}{2}\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{0}\sigma^{z}\Psi
−|N|​Ψ¯​σx​μx​Ψ+1g​∑μ=x,y(∂τAμ)2.\displaystyle-|N|\bar{\Psi}\sigma^{x}\mu^{x}\Psi+\frac{1}{g}\sum_{\mu=x,y}(\partial_{\tau}A_{\mu})^{2}. (15)

Now we can again perform the RPA, integrating out the fermions to quadratic order in AμA_{\mu} and ∂μθ\partial_{\mu}\theta. An explicit calculation is involved due to the need to regularize the Dirac theory, which must be done with care to maintain charge conservation and gauge invariance [45]. Fortunately, the result can be understood on the grounds of symmetries. The general form of the RPA effective action is

Seff\displaystyle S_{\rm eff} =12​∫d3​x​d3​x′\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int\!d^{3}xd^{3}x^{\prime}\,
×(Aμ​(x′)​∂μθ⁡(x′))​Πμ​ν​(x−x′)​(Aν​(x)∂νθ⁡(x)),\displaystyle\quad\times\left(A_{\mu}(x^{\prime})\;\partial_{\mu}\theta(x^{\prime})\right)\mathsf{\Pi}_{\mu\nu}(x-x^{\prime})\begin{pmatrix}A_{\nu}(x)\\ \partial_{\nu}\theta(x)\end{pmatrix}, (16)

where here x,x′x,x^{\prime} are space-time coordinates, and Πμ​ν\mathsf{\Pi}_{\mu\nu} is a generalized polarization tensor.

Owing to the presence of the gap in the fermion spectrum, the Fourier transform of the polarization must be analytic in frequency and momentum at scales below the gap, allowing a Taylor expansion. Furthermore, charge conservation (which enforces the continuity equation ∂μjμ=0\partial_{\mu}j_{\mu}=0 at the operator level) requires that ∂μΠμ​νA​A=∂νΠμ​νA​A=0\partial_{\mu}\mathsf{\Pi}^{AA}_{\mu\nu}=\partial_{\nu}\mathsf{\Pi}^{AA}_{\mu\nu}=0, and ∂μΠμ​νA​θ=∂νΠμ​νθ​A=0\partial_{\mu}\mathsf{\Pi}^{A\theta}_{\mu\nu}=\partial_{\nu}\mathsf{\Pi}^{\theta A}_{\mu\nu}=0, where the superscripts A,θA,\theta indicate the blocks within the polarization tensor. Assuming, as before, the temporal gauge A0=0A_{0}=0, writing the most general allowed form of the polarization tensor at lowest order in three-momenta, and Fourier transforming back to space-time, we obtain

ℒeff\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm eff} =14​c1​F0​j2+14​c2​Fi​j2+12​c3​(∂0θ)2+12​c4​(∂jθ)2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}c_{1}F_{0j}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}c_{2}F_{ij}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}c_{3}(\partial_{0}\theta)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}c_{4}(\partial_{j}\theta)^{2}
+i​c5​(∂iAi)​(∂0θ),\displaystyle+ic_{5}(\partial_{i}A_{i})(\partial_{0}\theta), (17)

where Fμ​ν=∂μAν−∂νAμF_{\mu\nu}=\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu}-\partial_{\nu}A_{\mu} is the field-strength tensor, i,ji,j indicate spatial indices and 00 is a time index. The constants c1−4>0c_{1-4}>0 for stability. The factor of ii in the last term is required by Hermiticity. The Lagrangian (17) is invariant under the residual gauge transformations Aj→Aj+∂jfA_{j}\to A_{j}+\partial_{j}f with τ\tau-independent ff. Finite frequency excitations of (17) are represented by the standard transverse mode with speed vT=2​c2/c1v_{T}=\sqrt{2c_{2}/c_{1}} and a longitudinal sound mode which mixes θ\theta and the longitudinal part of AA, with speed vL=(c4+2​c52/c1)/c3v_{L}=\sqrt{(c_{4}+2c_{5}^{2}/c_{1})/c_{3}}.

To illustrate the logic leading to the Lagrangian in (17), we comment on the last, cross term. Analyticity of Πμ​νA​θ\mathsf{\Pi}^{A\theta}_{\mu\nu} and charge conservation require that in the momentum space Πμ​νA​θ​(q)→Πμ​ν​λ(1)​qλ\mathsf{\Pi}^{A\theta}_{\mu\nu}(q)\to\mathsf{\Pi}^{(1)}_{\mu\nu\lambda}q_{\lambda}, where the coefficient of qq is a tensor of constants antisymmetric in indices μ,λ\mu,\lambda: Πμ​ν​λ(1)=ϵμ​λ​κ​cν​κ\mathsf{\Pi}^{(1)}_{\mu\nu\lambda}=\epsilon_{\mu\lambda\kappa}c_{\nu\kappa} and cν​κc_{\nu\kappa} are some constants. In space-time, this leads to cν​κ​ϵμ​λ​κ​∂λAμ​∂νθc_{\nu\kappa}\epsilon_{\mu\lambda\kappa}\partial_{\lambda}A_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}\theta. For cν​κ=δν​κc_{\nu\kappa}=\delta_{\nu\kappa}, this term vanishes. Naïvely, spatial rotation symmetry and time-reversal symmetry require c01=c02=0c_{01}=c_{02}=0, c12=−c21c_{12}=-c_{21} and c11=c22c_{11}=c_{22}. With this form, the c11=c22c_{11}=c_{22} contribution is a pure boundary term. Then, there remains c00≠0c_{00}\neq 0 term, and the above general form reduces to F12​∂0θF_{12}\partial_{0}\theta and Fi​0​∂iθF_{i0}\partial_{i}\theta and terms equivalent to these under integration by parts. We next observe that Eq. (15) is symmetric under paritylike transformation x→−x,Ax→−Ax,Ψ→γx​μz​Ψx\to-x,A_{x}\to-A_{x},\Psi\to\gamma^{x}\mu^{z}\Psi and Ψ¯→−Ψ¯​γx​μz\bar{\Psi}\to-\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{x}\mu^{z}, which, however, changes the sign of the flux F12→−F12F_{12}\to-F_{12} and rules out the first option but preserves the second one, ∝∂iAi​∂0θ\propto\partial_{i}A_{i}\partial_{0}\theta.

The Lagrangian in Eq. (17) is a coupled Maxwell theory for AμA_{\mu} and a free massless scalar field theory for θ\theta, which describes two massless linearly dispersing modes. The presence of two such modes indicates that both the U(1)m and U(1)f symmetries are spontaneously broken in the AFM phase. The gapless θ\theta mode will appear as a spin-wave-like mode in the transverse spin structure factor, with high intensity as it approaches the Bragg peak associated with the AFM order (we show our DQMC results for the transverse magnetic spectra in Sec. IV.3).

Because of the presence of the gapless photon, we also expect power-law correlations of the flux in the AFM phase, of the same form as in the CF phase (but distinct from those in the DSL). We refer the reader to our DQMC results for temporal flux correlation functions in Sec. IV of the SM [36]. These power-law flux correlations, together with the gapless spin-wave branch in the structure factor, are signatures of the two broken symmetries of the AFM state.

III Phase diagram

Our numerically obtained phase diagram is presented in Fig. 1 (b). At zero magnetic field, there exists a stable Dirac spin liquid phase, which is a nontrivial critical phase in which a configuration with π\pi-flux of the gauge field on each plaquette is dynamically selected. Such a small-JJ DSL phase has also been reported in the compact case in Ref. [33]. There are theoretical arguments which indicate the DSL is unstable in the compact case (see Sec. V). We conclude there are strong finite-size effects which affect the compact model, since for a 20×2020\times 20 lattice, the expected power-law correlations of the fermion bilinears in spin operators with decay exponent of 2​Δ∼32\Delta\sim 3 (see Sec. II.3.1) inside DSL phase have been observed. Similarly, the finite extent of the DSL phase for B>0B>0 in Fig. 1 (b) is due to the nonzero temperature accessible in our simulations. We expect the DSL to give way to the CF phase for infinitesimal Zeeman fields in the zero-temperature thermodynamic limit.

At finite BB, the flux per plaquette starts to deviate from π\pi and the system enters a chiral flux phase. In this phase the Néel order parameter N+N^{+} remains zero, but the flux per plaquette deviates from π\pi (and 00). Two possible distinct states – with flux in (0,π)(0,\pi) or in (π,2​π)(\pi,2\pi) – are possible, one of which is spontaneously chosen, resulting in spontaneous breaking of the time-reversal symmetry 𝒯\mathcal{T}. This is characterized by the chiral order parameter ⟨sin⁡Φ□⟩\langle\sin\Phi_{\Box}\rangle. We stress that 𝒯\mathcal{T} is broken due to the nontrivial gauge flux in the system: in contrast, a finite Zeeman field or spin polarization at vanishing flux preserves 𝒯\mathcal{T}. As discussed in Sec. II.3.2, there is also a more subtle breaking of U(1)m×{}_{m}\timesU(1)f symmetry, which is reflected in a gapless photon mode and the nonzero susceptibility of the CF phase.

As will be further discussed in Sec. III.2, one can define a scale-invariant correlation ratio UfluxU_{\text{flux}} of the chiral order and at finite BB and small JJ, one sees that UfluxU_{\text{flux}} is large while the correlation ratio of the antiferromagnetic phase rAFMr_{\text{AFM}} is small (meaning no antiferromagnetic long-range order). While at finite BB and large JJ, the trend is opposite, suggesting the vanishing of the CF order and the establishment of the U(1)f symmetry breaking in the form of an antiferromagnetic long-range order in the x−yx-y components (AFM). To clearly discuss these results, we first provide the mean-field analysis of the phase diagram at J=0J=0 and then discuss the DQMC results at finite JJ.

III.1 Mean-field analysis at J=0J=0

The deviation from π\pi-flux at nonzero Zeeman field can be demonstrated by a mean field analysis of the lattice model, which forms a basis for understanding the DQMC results. The mean-field approximation consists of neglecting the dynamics of the gauge field, i.e. assuming ai​j​(τn)a_{ij}(\tau_{n}) is independent of τn\tau_{n}. Inspecting the final term in Eq. (1), one sees that this approximation becomes exact in the limit J→0J\rightarrow 0, as configurations of the gauge field with any time dependence have infinite action in this limit. The fermionic path integral for a particular time-independent flux configuration gives, then, simply the free fermion partition function with this flux. At zero temperature (β→∞\beta\rightarrow\infty), this is exp⁡(−β​E0​(Φ□))\exp(-\beta E_{0}(\Phi_{\Box})), where E0​(Φ□)E_{0}(\Phi_{\Box}) is the fermionic ground state energy with the given flux, and hence the flux becomes (in the thermodynamic and zero temperature limits) constrained to take the value which minimizes the energy. To find the latter, we manually set the flux of each plaquette in Landau gauge and calculate the energies as a sum of the fermion kinetic energy and the Zeeman energy. The input parameters of the mean-field calculation are the Zeeman field BB, which acts like an opposite chemical potential for fermion with opposite spin, and the flux sector Φ□\Phi_{\Box}, which in turn determines the gauge field within Landau gauge, which we choose. We can then construct and diagonalize the fermion hopping matrix, whose eigenvalues, the single-particle energies, are shown in Fig. 2(a) for different flux sectors. The Zeeman field BB controls the filling of the fermions, from which we obtain the magnetization mz=1N​∑iN12​(ni,↑−ni,↓)m_{z}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}^{N}\frac{1}{2}(n_{i,\uparrow}-n_{i,\downarrow}). We then can obtain the total energy of the system as a function of the specific flux sector Φ□\Phi_{\Box} and Zeeman field BB, from which we extract the flux sector with minimal energy. We observe a significant deviation from π\pi-flux for nonzero Zeeman field. The conclusion is consistent with the mean-field analysis in Ref. [31] for a Kagomé lattice model.

The flux sector corresponding to the minimum energy versus Zeeman field is shown in Fig. 2(c). At zero Zeeman field, the system favors the π\pi-flux gauge field arrangement. However, for nonzero Zeeman field, the favorable flux sectors deviate from π\pi-flux and are symmetric about π\pi-flux from Fig. 2(b) data, indicating broken 𝒯\mathcal{T} symmetry. By interpreting ±B/2\pm B/2 as an opposite chemical potential for up and down fermions, the Φ□\Phi_{\Box} vs B/tB/t relation gives the spin-dependent Fermi levels, shown in Fig. 2(a) by red and green lines. In this plot, spin up and down fermions occupy states below the red and green levels, respectively. In Fig. 2(d), we show π−Φ□\pi-\Phi_{\Box} vs magnetization mzm_{z}, which demonstrates a linear relation. The constant slope indicates that the bands between the two Fermi levels have a fixed total Chern number of 1 for the full range of fields.

III.2 DQMC simulations with J≠0J\neq 0

With J≠0J\neq 0, the fluctuations of the gauge field render the problem in Eq. (1) strongly correlated and one has to rely on the DQMC results. As mentioned in Sec. II.1, in our DQMC lattice simulations, we denote the system size of the cubic lattice in Fig. 1(a) by LL and β\beta. We scan the phase diagram in the unit of B/tB/t and J/tJ/t and scale the inverse temperature β=1T=2​L\beta=\frac{1}{T}=2L so that we approach zero temperature in the large system limit (in our setting Δ​τ=0.1\Delta\tau=0.1 and the integer index in the temporal direction Nτ=β/Δ​τ=20​LN_{\tau}=\beta/\Delta\tau=20L).

To analyze the symmetry breaking patterns, we consider both chiral flux and antiferromagnetic orders. We first verify that the chiral flux (CF) order is uniform and that the antiferromagnetism is the standard two-sublattice staggered type by considering their corresponding equal time structure factors. For the chiral order, this is

Sχ(𝐪)=1N□∑i,j⟨sin(Φ□,i)sin(Φ□,j)⟩e−i𝐪⋅𝐫i​j,S_{\chi}(\mathbf{q})=\frac{1}{N_{\Box}}\sum_{i,j}\langle\sin(\Phi_{\Box,i})\sin(\Phi_{\Box,j})\rangle e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{ij}}, (18)

where N□=L2N_{\Box}=L^{2} is the number of plaquettes. i,ji,j are the position of plaquettes labeled by their lower left-hand site. The maximum of SχS_{\chi} fixes the ordering wave vector, which is at 𝐪=Γ\mathbf{q}=\Gamma. For the AFM order, the corresponding (transverse) equal time spin structure factor is

S±(𝐪)=1N∑i​j⟨Si+Sj−+h.c.⟩e−i𝐪⋅𝐫i​jS^{\pm}(\mathbf{q})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{ij}\langle S^{+}_{i}S^{-}_{j}+h.c.\rangle\ e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{ij}} (19)

where Si+=ci,↑†​ci,↓S^{+}_{i}=c^{\dagger}_{i,\uparrow}c_{i,\downarrow}, Si−=ci,↓†​ci,↑S^{-}_{i}=c^{\dagger}_{i,\downarrow}c_{i,\uparrow} and N=L2N=L^{2}. The maximum structure factor again fixes the ordering wave vector, which is at the 𝑴=(π,π)\bm{M}=(\pi,\pi) point for the AFM and the AFM order parameter discussed in Sec. II.3.3, |N+|=limN→∞S±​(𝑴)/(2​N)|N^{+}|=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sqrt{S^{\pm}(\bm{M})/(2N)}.

With the ordering wave vectors determined, we proceed to find the phase boundaries in the JJ-BB plane by choosing appropriate measures of the two order parameters. An example of data and analysis for a cut at fixed B/t=2B/t=2 is shown in Fig. 3. For the chiral order (panel (a)), we measure the Binder cumulant of the sine of the flux on a plaquette. We define fχ=1N□​∑□sin⁡(Φ□)f_{\chi}=\frac{1}{N_{\Box}}\sum_{\Box}\sin(\Phi_{\Box}) and then the Binder cumulant UfluxU_{\text{flux}} is

Uflux=1−⟨fχ4⟩3​⟨fχ2⟩2.U_{\text{flux}}=1-\frac{\langle f_{\chi}^{4}\rangle}{3\langle f_{\chi}^{2}\rangle^{2}}. (20)

Inside the CF phase, Uflux→23U_{\text{flux}}\to\frac{2}{3} and once the 𝒯\mathcal{T} symmetry is recovered, for example, by increasing JJ with fixed BB, Uflux→0U_{\text{flux}}\to 0. Hence a crossing is expected in the thermodynamic limit within a plot of UfluxU_{\text{flux}} along a line crossing the boundary between a phase with chiral order (broken 𝒯\mathcal{T}) and one without.

For the antiferromagnetic order, we use dimensionless correlation ratio

rAFM=1−S±​(𝐪+δ​𝐪)S±​(𝐪)r_{\text{AFM}}=1-\frac{S^{\pm}(\mathbf{q}+\delta\mathbf{q})}{S^{\pm}(\mathbf{q})} (21)

in which 𝐪=M\mathbf{q}=M is the ordering wave vector and 𝐪+δ​𝐪\mathbf{q}+\delta\mathbf{q} is the closest adjacent wave vector in momentum space. In the disordered phase, rAFM→0r_{\text{AFM}}\to 0 as the structure is flat in the momentum space, and in the ordered phase rAFM→1r_{\text{AFM}}\to 1, once the Bragg peak at 𝐪\mathbf{q} is fully developed in the thermodynamic limit. Like for the Binder ratio of CF order, we thus expect a crossing of rAFMr_{\text{AFM}} on cuts crossing the phase boundary between AFM ordered and disordered regions, for large system sizes, as shown in Fig. 3 (b) for B/t=2B/t=2 case.

The results of this analysis using multiple cuts are summarized in the phase diagram in Fig. 1(b). We observe substantial regions with CF order, AFM order, and a small overlapping region in which both CF and AFM order coexist. We will present and discuss the magnetic spectra in CF and AFM phases in Sec. IV.

Before doing so, we check the DQMC simulations for evidence of the gauge field dynamics. To this end, we consider the dynamical flux correlation function

Cχ​(τ)=1N□​∑□⟨sin⁡(Φ□​(τ))​sin⁡(Φ□​(0))⟩.C_{\chi}(\tau)=\frac{1}{N_{\Box}}\sum_{\Box}\langle\sin(\Phi_{\Box}(\tau))\sin(\Phi_{\Box}(0))\rangle. (22)

Fig. 4 shows the imaginary time decay of the Cχ​(τ)C_{\chi}(\tau) at B/t=3B/t=3 as a function of JJ. For small J/t<1J/t<1 (inside CF phase) the decay saturates to a constant at “large” τ\tau, indicating the presence of spontaneous chiral order. At large J/t>1J/t>1 (inside AFM phase), it decays to a negligible value. However, even well in the AFM phase, e.g. J/t=3J/t=3, the form of the decay is clearly subexponential. This indicates power-law correlations consistent with the expected gapless photon mode (see Sec. II.3.3). In fact, as shown in Sec. IV of the SM [36], our DQMC simulations find the flux correlation functions inside the AFM phase as Cχ​(τ)∼τ−3C_{\chi}(\tau)\sim\tau^{-3} and for the DSL phase as Cχ​(τ)∼τ−4C_{\chi}(\tau)\sim\tau^{-4}, consistent with theoretical expectations. For comparison, we also plot the same flux correlator for the compact model [33] for J/t=3,B/t=0J/t=3,B/t=0 (inside the confined AFM phase). One can clearly see exponential decay in that case, which is due to confinement physics that is absent in the mixed model. While it is difficult to separate the power-law decay from the saturation within the CF phase, a power-law approach to the large-time saturation is also expected in these cases as well. We conclude that through the phase diagram, the gauge field is “deconfined” in the mixed model.

IV Magnetic spectra

A key implication of the generation of a finite flux of the emergent gauge field is that the Dirac fermions experience an orbital magnetic field and form Landau levels [7]. While the single-spinon spectrum is not gauge-invariant, one may inspect how the formation of such Landau levels impacts the dynamic spin structure factor, where we consider both the transverse component S±​(ω,𝒒)=1N​∑i​j∫d​t​⟨Si+​(t)​Sj−​(0)+Si−​(t)​Sj+​(0)⟩​ei⁡(ω​t−𝒒⋅𝒓i​j)S^{\pm}(\omega,\bm{q})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{ij}\int\mathrm{d}t\langle S^{+}_{i}(t)S^{-}_{j}(0)+S^{-}_{i}(t)S^{+}_{j}(0)\rangle\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\omega t-\bm{q}\cdot\bm{r}_{ij})} as well as the longitudinal component Sz​z​(ω,𝒒)S^{zz}(\omega,\bm{q}). Formally, in the zero-temperature limit, the dynamic structure factor can be obtained via the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, Sa(ω,𝒒)=−2Θ(ω)Imχa(iω→ω+i0+,𝒒)S^{a}(\omega,\bm{q})=-2\Theta(\omega)\operatorname{Im}\chi^{a}(\mathrm{i}\omega\to\omega+\mathrm{i}0^{+},\bm{q}) from the dynamical susceptibility (i.e. response) χa​(i​ω,𝒒)\chi^{a}(\mathrm{i}\omega,\bm{q}) to an external probe field which couples to the spin density at momentum 𝒒\bm{q} (see also the discussion in Sec. II.3). Since the fermionic spinons carry S=1/2S=1/2 quantum numbers, this susceptibility can be obtained from dynamical response of the fermionic degrees of freedom. Below, we first infer key qualitative features of the dynamic spin structure factor in a mean-field approximation (both in the continuum limit, where an analytical treatment is feasible and on the square lattice geometry), and then present magnetic spectra in the CF phase upon including gauge fluctuations obtained from our DQMC simulations.

At these points, in the zero-field limit, the magnetic spectrum is dominated by particle-hole excitations on top of the single-particle Dirac cones.
