and similarly for the longitudinal component. Here, 𝒌\bm{k} refers to small momenta close to the high-symmetry points 𝑸=𝚪,𝑿\bm{Q}=\bm{\Gamma},\bm{X} and 𝑴\bm{M}. The choice of lattice momentum 𝑸\bm{Q} is encoded in the vertices that enter the bubble diagram – these are determined by starting from a microscopic lattice model and making a gradient expansion to read off how microscopic lattice translation or rotation symmetries act on the sublattice and valley indices of the Dirac fermions (we refer the reader to Sec. I of the SM [36] for a lattice expression of this diagram, and Sec. II of the SM [36] for technical details concerning our continuum field-theory calculations). Further, in Eq. (23), the dots correspond to corrections arising from interactions with the emergent U(1) gauge field.

We henceforth work on a “bare” level and neglect such interactions with the U(1) gauge field, corresponding to a mean-field approximation. For an effective RPA-level treatment of the fluctuating gauge field, see Sec. II.3.

We first give a physical picture for possible excitations that can give rise to poles in the structure factor: noting the low-energy expressions of the spin operators in terms of spinon fields listed in Eqs. (S11a)–(S11c) of Sec. II of the SM [36], applying the spin-lowering operator S−∼ψ↓†​ψ↑S^{-}\sim\psi^{\dagger}_{\downarrow}\psi_{\uparrow} on top of the ground state with spin-split Landau levels can be seen to create a hole in a filled spin-↑\uparrow Landau level and create a particle in an otherwise empty spin-↓\downarrow Landau level. This is illustrated in Fig. 5. Transitions belonging to the same (spin-split) Landau level are in general not allowed (as they are fully occupied or empty for |n|>0|n|>0), except in the 0-th Landau level, of which only the spin-↑\uparrow copy is filled (for b>0b>0). This excitation corresponds to a pole at frequency ω=b\omega=b in the transverse contribution to the structure factor. Conversely, now consider the action S+∼ψ↑†​ψ↓S^{+}\sim\psi^{\dagger}_{\uparrow}\psi_{\downarrow} on top of the ground state with b≥0b\geq 0. Creating a spin-↓\downarrow hole and a spin-↑\uparrow particle is allowed only if they respectively occur in Landau levels |n|≥1|n|\geq 1, such that these particle-hole excitations can occur only with energies ω=En+Em−b\omega=E_{n}+E_{m}-b with n,m≥1n,m\geq 1.

In contrast to the transverse response, the longitudinal susceptibility, and thus the structure factor, will involve excitations that preserve the magnetization. Hence, only inter-Landau-level transition are allowed. These can in general give rise to poles at frequencies ω=En+Em\omega=E_{n}+E_{m}, where n,m≥0n,m\geq 0 (but not n=m=0n=m=0).

With a qualitative understanding of excitations (in the mean-field limit) that can give rise to poles in the transverse and longitudinal structure factors, we now turn to their respective spectral weights at the 𝚪,𝑴\bm{\Gamma},\bm{M} and 𝑿\bm{X} points, where the spinon particle-hole excitations dominate the low-energy response. We obtain the spectral weights via an explicit evaluation of Eq. (23), with technical details provided in Sec. II of the SM [36].

We note the following key predictions from our field-theoretical analysis:

  1. 1.

    At the 𝚪\bm{\Gamma}-point, only the pole of frequency ω=b\omega=b contributes finite spectral weight to the transverse structure factor (arising from spin-flip particle-hole excitations in the spin-split 0th-Landau level). This is in accordance with Larmor’s theorem: since the ground state (at zero field b=0b=0) is SU(2)-symmetric, the only dynamic response to the SU(2)-breaking Zeeman field bb consists in a transverse spin wave with frequency bb, with the spectral weight determined by the system’s magnetization mzm^{z} [47, 48, 49], ⟨S+​S−+S−​S+⟩​(ω,𝚪)=4​π​mz​δ​(ω−b)\langle S^{+}S^{-}+S^{-}S^{+}\rangle(\omega,\bm{\Gamma})=4\pi m^{z}\delta(\omega-b). We further note that this mode of frequency bb also has finite spectral weight in the transverse structure factor at 𝑴\bm{M} (in addition to many other modes), while it is absent in S±S^{\pm} at the 𝑿\bm{X}-point.

  2. 2.

    Turning to the longitudinal structure factor Sz​zS^{zz}, poles occur at energies proportional to the cyclotron frequency (which is a priori independent of the Zeeman-energy). We find that Sz​z​(𝚪,ω)=0S^{zz}(\bm{\Gamma},\omega)=0, consistent with Larmor’s theorem (see above). We further observe that all low-energy poles at the 𝑿\bm{X}-point (i.e. ω=E1,E1+E2,…\omega=E_{1},E_{1}+E_{2},\dots) generally carry finite weight, while poles with finite weight at the 𝑴\bm{M}-point occur at much higher frequencies, i.e. ω=2​E1,2​E2​…\omega=2E_{1},2E_{2}\dots.

  3. 3.

    One may further find the structure factor at finite (small) momenta 𝒒\bm{q} relative to these high-symmetry points. We have explicitly obtained S𝚪±​(𝒒,ω)S^{\pm}_{\bm{\Gamma}}(\bm{q},\omega), shown in Fig. 6, see also Sec. II of the SM [36] for details: Going away from 𝚪\bm{\Gamma}, other poles (in addition to the Larmor mode) generally acquire finite spectral weight. Here, ⟨S+​S−⟩\langle S^{+}S^{-}\rangle contains poles with frequencies ω≥b\omega\geq b, while ⟨S−​S+⟩\langle S^{-}S^{+}\rangle may contain poles with energies below the Larmor mode. The maximum spectral weight at a given frequency follows a linear dispersion νmax.​(𝒌)=|𝒌|+b\nu_{\mathrm{max.}}(\bm{k})=|\bm{k}|+b – this is consistent with continuity arguments wherein going toward the zero-field limit the Landau levels become dense, and linearly dispersing cones emerge in the structure factor (resulting from particle-hole excitations on the spinon Dirac cones).

Below, we compare these insights based on a low-energy theory (assuming a static gauge field) with our numerical results.

IV.2 Lattice mean-field calculations

We now turn to the lattice action in Eq. (1). In the limit of static gauge field, J=0J=0, we perform lattice mean-field calculations (see Sec. I of the SM [36] for details)

Our results for the real-frequency transverse and longitudinal spin structure factors are shown along a high-symmetry path in the Brillouin zone in Fig. 7(a) and  8(a), and detailed energy scans at a few representative momenta are shown in Fig. 9.

We first note that the lattice mean-field spectra (both transverse and longitudinal) exhibit a fine structure of many separate nearly dispersionless bands. Equipped with theoretical analysis in Secs. II.3.2 and IV.1, this discrete spectrum can be directly attributed to inter- or intra-Landau-level transitions. We further observe that the individual bands in the transverse (longitudinal) can be grouped into three (four) sets. We attribute this additional structure to lattice effects that lie beyond our continuum field-theory analysis.

Transverse structure factor.

Comparing to our field-theoretic predictions [points (1) and (3) in Sec. IV.1], we observe that exactly at the 𝚪\bm{\Gamma}-point, there is only a single mode (at frequency ω=3​t=B\omega=3t=B) in the transverse structure factor which carries finite weight – this is precisely the Larmor mode. For small momenta near the 𝚪\bm{\Gamma}-point, additional modes with finite weight emerge, and we observe that there is a linear scaling for the frequency of the spectra weight onset as a function of momenta 𝒒\bm{q} as a remnant of the linear dispersion of the Dirac fermions in the zero-field case. We further note the low-frequency response at the 𝑴\bm{M}-point features rather intense spectral weight, as visible in Fig. 7(a) and in Fig. 9(b). This low-energy spectral weight could be an indication of the eventual emergence of a Goldstone magnon at the 𝑴\bm{M}-point in the AFM phase, upon increasing the interaction strength.

Longitudinal structure factor.

A particularly striking feature of the longitudinal structure factor in Fig. 8(a) at the 𝑴\bm{M} point is the full concentration of spectral weight in the topmost bands, at frequencies ω/t∼5\omega/t\sim 5 (and a concomitant absence of weight at low and intermediate frequencies). This strong concentration of weight at large frequencies becomes also visible when inspecting the line cuts at the 𝑴\bm{M}-point in Fig. 9(d). We argue this to be consistent with our field-theoretic finding that many poles in Sz​z​(ω)S^{zz}(\omega) have vanishing spectral weight at the 𝑴\bm{M}-point.

IV.3 QMC plus stochastic analytic continuation (SAC) simulations

For finite J≠0J\neq 0 we obtain the imaginary-time correlation function from our DQMC simulations and then perform a stochastic analytic continuation (SAC) to obtain the real-frequency results [50, 51, 52, 53]. This QMC+SAC scheme has been applied to a variety of lattice models, including the Dirac fermions under Hubbard-type interaction and the magnetic field [49], producing reliable spectral properties ranging from magnon and amplitude modes in a magnetically ordered state [54, 55], fractionalized excitations in quantum spin liquid and spin ice models [56, 57, 58], as well as an emergent Dirac spinon spectrum at deconfined quantum critical points [59] and single-particle spectrum of the angle-tuned Gross-Neveu quantum criticality in twisted bilayer graphene [60].

Qualitative effect of small J>0J>0.

In comparing the QMC+SAC spectra (with small nonzero J/t=0.1J/t=0.1) to the mean-field spectra (with J=0J=0), we observe two main effects beyond the mean-field. First, the non-mean-field spectra are broadened relative to the finely discretized nature of the mean-field spectra associated with inter- or intra-Landau-level excitations. This is expected on general grounds: the interaction with the fluctuating gauge field will yield a broadening (finite lifetimes) of both single-particle spectra as well as the two-particle response functions. Second, in some spectral functions (see below) new collective modes emerge below the support of the mean-field spectra.

However, we note that even in the presence of such broadening, the DQMC structure factors in Fig. 7(b) and Fig. 8(b) possess several bandlike high-intensity features that resemble the lattice mean-field spectra in Fig. 7(a) and Fig. 8(a). This correspondence is further corroborated by inspecting the line cuts in Fig. 9. We stress that the key qualitative features identified in the continuum field theory and lattice mean-field calculations above persist also at finite interaction strengths.

Transverse structure factor in the CF phase.

In this component of the structure factor, the main difference of the mean-field and J/t=0.1J/t=0.1 spectra is the broadening. However, broadening is absent, as is seen from Fig. 7(b), at the 𝚪\bm{\Gamma}-point, where there is a sharp mode at frequency ω=3​t\omega=3t: this is the Larmor mode, with frequency ω=B\omega=B and weight 4​π​mz4\pi m^{z} protected against interactions. Going away from the 𝚪\bm{\Gamma}-point, one can further observe a linear dispersion ω⁡(𝒌)∼|𝒌|\omega(\bm{k})\sim|\bm{k}| of the spectral weight, in line with our theoretical predictions.

Longitudinal structure factor in the CF phase.

At the 𝑴\bm{M}-point, there is a strong concentration of spectral weight in the longitudinal structure factor near ω≃5​t\omega\simeq 5t, and vanishing spectral weight at all other frequencies (see Fig. 8(b) and Fig. 9(d)), in qualitative agreement with our continuum field theory and lattice mean-field calculations. We further comment that such a concentration of spectral weight at high frequencies at the 𝑴\bm{M}-point is reminiscent of the high-energy single-magnon excitation in the high-field regime of the square-lattice antiferromagnet which emerges upon increasing the interaction strength J/tJ/t [61, 62].

In the longitudinal structure factor, the J/t=0.1J/t=0.1 spectra clearly exhibit a low-energy collective mode near Γ\Gamma not present in the corresponding mean-field spectra – compare Fig. 8 panels (a) and (b). Although the finite-size and finite-temperature effects (L=β=16L=\beta=16) prevent us from resolving the predicted linear dispersion quantitatively, the observed low-energy spectral weight near Γ\Gamma is consistent with, but does not by itself establish, the photon-related response expected from Eq. (11) in Sec. II.3.2. Very similar spectra, inside the CF phase at B/t=2B/t=2, are shown in Sec. VII of the SM [36].

Structure factor in the U(1) DSL phase.

We show the magnetic spectra in π\pi-flux U(1) deconfined phase (mixed theory) at zero Zeeman field (B=0B=0) in Fig. 10(a), which demonstrates well-known continuum characteristics with gapless Dirac cones at the 𝚪\bm{\Gamma}, 𝑿\bm{X} and 𝑴\bm{M}-points. The spectra can be qualitatively reproduced by a simple RPA calculation of the noninteracting structure factor of the π\pi-flux fermion hopping model [59]. However, a quantitative analysis shows the effects of gauge fluctuations. Specifically, we have also computed the real-space spin correlation function inside the DSL phase up to L=20L=20. As shown in Fig. 10(b), our data exhibit a power-law decay with exponent 2​ΔS=3.2​(1)2\Delta_{S}=3.2(1), consistent with the expectation of 2​Δa​d​j∈(2.8,3.5)2\Delta_{adj}\in(2.8,3.5) for the fermion bilinear operators in the CFT of SU(4) QED3, discussed in Sec. II.3.1. We note that similar power-law spin and dimer correlations with the exponent of 2​Δ∼32\Delta\sim 3 have also been seen in the DSL phase in Ref. [33]. For comparison, real-space correlations inside CF and AFM phase with Zeeman field B/t=2B/t=2 are shown in Fig. 10. Both display non-power-law decay, with fast decay in CF phase which indicates short-range transverse spin correlations and gapped transverse spectra. In AFM, spin correlations show long-range order.

Magnetic spectra in the AFM phase.

When J/tJ/t is larger, there can be substantial deviations from the mean-field spectrum. Physically, the probability for fermions to bind or recombine into collective modes becomes large, and such modes may be more dominant in the spectral response. The QMC+SAC results for the transverse and longitudinal spectra in the AFM phase at J/t=3J/t=3 for B/t=3B/t=3 are shown in Fig. 11. In Fig. 11(a), one observes spin-wave-like features near 𝑴\bm{M} point, with the 𝑴\bm{M}-point itself hosting a gapless Goldstone mode (see also Sec. II.3.3). In Fig. 11(b), the longitudinal spectrum is fully gapped, and in particular there is a high-intensity feature (ω/t≈3\omega/t\approx 3) at the ordering wave vector 𝑴\bm{M}. This feature is similar to that of the Heisenberg square-lattice antiferromagnet in strong Zeeman fields [62, 61], which has only localized bosonic states. This is in agreement with a picture of substantial recombination of the fermions into bosonic local excitations.

V Discussion

In this work, we have studied the response of QED3 to a flavor chemical potential, which emerges in a condensed matter context as the low-energy theory for the response of a U(1) Dirac spin liquid to an externally applied Zeeman field.

Utilizing large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations for the case of a mixed gauge field, we unambiguously establish that for finite flavor chemical potentials (Zeeman field), there exists a stable “chiral flux” phase which is characterized by the emergent gauge field developing a finite net average flux, with the system’s magnetization being proportional to the induced flux, mz∝π−Φ□m^{z}\propto\pi-\Phi_{\Box}.

V.1 Key results and implications

The field-induced generation of emergent gauge flux has several key implications:

  1. 1.

    The fermionic spectrum of the theory is given by spin-split relativistic Landau-Hofstadter levels and thus becomes gapped. The transverse and longitudinal magnetic structure factors exhibit signatures of the Landau-level spectrum, and we match a number of qualitative features obtained within a continuum field-theory analysis with our numerical results, for example the presence of a Larmor mode in the transverse magnetic structure factor [48, 49].

  2. 2.

    Owing to the suppression of monopoles in the time-continuum limit (see [36] for an explicit demonstration in an analytically tractable model) in the model at hand, the U(1) gauge field remains coherent in the CF phase and features a gapless photon excitation. The effective theory predicts a photon-related low-energy contribution to the longitudinal magnetic structure factor. The QMC+SAC spectra show low-energy spectral weight near Γ\Gamma consistent with this expectation; further work is required to resolve the predicted linear dispersion quantitatively. Such a response also distinguishes the strongly correlated nature of the CF phase at finite JJ, that is beyond the mean-field analysis at J=0J=0.

  3. 3.

    In an effective field-theory framework, the CF state can be described by a mixed Chern-Simons term for fluctuations of the emergent gauge field and an external “spin” gauge field, which encodes the attachment of spin SzS^{z} to flux of the emergent gauge field. This implies that the CF state is characterized by a composite order parameter ⟨ℳ​S+⟩≠0\langle\mathcal{M}S^{+}\rangle\neq 0, where ℳ\mathcal{M} is a 2​π2\pi-gauge flux insertion operator. This is consistent with our numerical observation that the transverse spin spectra show a full gap in the CF phase.

We argue that these results are directly related to the generation of a finite flux in the QED3 gauge theory. Connecting with quantum magnets, we stipulate that observing such behavior of a quantum spin liquid candidate material in an applied magnetic field would be hard to reconcile with more conventional descriptions (i.e. which do not rely on fractionalization and emergent gauge fields).

V.2 Effects due to dynamical monopoles

When QED3 arises as an emergent gauge field in a microscopic spin model, the theory is inevitably fully periodic in the gauge field. In general, this allows dynamical monopole instantons, which are suppressed in our study. It is known that monopoles carry distinct quantum numbers under different microscopic (lattice-scale) symmetries [10, 11], and that their presence may have severe consequences for the stability of U(1) Dirac spin liquids at the lowest energies on different lattices. The similarity of the results in this paper at zero field for the mixed theory to zero field simulations of the compact theory in Ref. [33, 64] suggests, however, that such effects may become significant only at very low (and vanishing in some cases) energy scales. We leave a quantitative analysis of such very low energy effects to future (numerical) work. This limitation does not affect the controlled conclusion of the present work: within the mixed theory, the field-induced chiral-flux phase and its characteristic dynamical spin-response signatures are established numerically. The following discussion instead addresses how monopole effects may modify this physics in a fully compact gauge theory.

While abovementioned effects are crucial for understanding the stability of U(1) Dirac spin liquids in general, we now turn to the central object of study in this paper, namely the field-induced chiral flux phase with nonzero gauge flux: here, the eventually inevitable compactness of the U(1) gauge field, and the associated monopole excitations will have a particularly prominent effect. We argue that they render the “hidden” order (of joint 2​π2\pi flux insertion and simultaneous change of Δ​Sz=1\Delta S^{z}=1, see also Sec. II.3.2 and in particular Eqs. (12) and (13) therein) to be physical, thus allowing it to be resolved in terms of experimentally accessible local order parameters. To demonstrate this, we posit that one may relate expectation values of observables ⟨𝒪⟩comp\langle\mathcal{O}\rangle_{\mathrm{comp}} in the full compact theory (with dynamical monopoles) to expectation values in the mixed theory (absent of monopoles) by means of an expansion in the monopole fugacity λ\lambda, i.e., we deform the action of the mixed theory by 2​π2\pi flux insertion operators, 𝒮mix→𝒮mix−∫d3​x​[λ​ℳ+λ∗​ℳ†]\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{mix}}\to\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{mix}}-\int d^{3}x[\lambda\mathcal{M}+\lambda^{\ast}\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}] (for simplicity, we adopt a continuum formulation, but the argument also applies to discretized space-time). Now, consider the in-plane spin density S+S^{+} as an observable. As argued in Sec. II.3.2, in the mixed theory ⟨S+⟩mix=0\langle S^{+}\rangle_{\mathrm{mix}}=0 vanishes in the chiral flux phase. However, in the compact theory, we observe

⟨S+​(x)⟩comp=⟨S+​(x)⟩mix+∫d3yλ⟨S+(x)ℳ(y)⟩mix+… ≈+λ⟨S+(x)ℳ(x)⟩mix≠0.\langle S^{+}(x)\rangle_{\mathrm{comp}}=\langle S^{+}(x)\rangle_{\mathrm{mix}}\\ {}+\int d^{3}y\,\lambda\langle S^{+}(x)\mathcal{M}(y)\rangle_{\mathrm{mix}}+\dots{\\ }\approx+\lambda\langle S^{+}(x)\mathcal{M}(x)\rangle_{\mathrm{mix}}\neq 0. (24)

The fugacity expansion (to leading order) thus produces the composite order parameter which, within the mixed theory, is finite in the chiral flux phase: therefore, the presence of dynamical monopoles in the fully compact theory makes the hidden composite order in the chiral flux phase visible as finite in-plane magnetic order.

We emphasize that the nature of the in-plane magnetic order, for example the ordering wave vector, will depend on the UV details of the theory which determine how the microscopic symmetries act on the low-energy degrees of freedom in the QED3 field theory. For the challenges elucidated above, a controlled study of this monopole-induced effect within numerical simulations of the QED3 low-energy field theory appears challenging at present. However, from a complementary standpoint, one may construct microscopic (variational) wave functions associated with a “chiral flux” state by Gutzwiller-projecting Slater determinants of fermionic spinons on a lattice, thereby accounting for aforementioned UV details. A recent analysis [65] of such a family of finite-flux wave functions for triangular-lattice systems has indeed revealed highly pronounced antiferromagnetic (120 ∘) in-plane spin correlations, consistent with the general field-theoretic argument provided above.

V.3 Outlook

We note that recently several candidate materials have been identified that exhibit signatures consistent with a (proximate) U(1) Dirac spin liquid ground state, such as the triangular-lattice antiferromagnets YbZn2GaO5 [66, 67] and the AA-YbSe2 delafossites [68, 69] as well as the kagomé antiferromagnet YCu3(OD)6Br2[Brx(OD)1-x] [70, 71, 18, 72], where inelastic neutron scattering experiments have found spectra that are consistent with a Dirac cone filled with a continuum of excitations. In light of our results, it will be highly interesting to scrutinize the behavior of these systems in applied magnetic fields. In particular, we foresee the experimental observation of a gapless magnetic spectral feature related to the photon mode in the longitudinal spin structure factor, possibly via inelastic neutron scattering, to be interesting evidence of the magnetized DSL state. An interesting direction for further study is to investigate what perturbations might lead to different filling of the spinon Landau levels in the CF phase (while maintaining gauge invariance or particle-hole symmetry), and establish possible connections to experimentally observed unusual magnetic oscillations in the YCu3(OD)6Br2[Brx(OD)1-x] kagomé antiferromagnet [73] (see also Ref. [74]).

Going beyond quantum magnets, we stress that our main result, the generation of the Chiral Flux phase due to a flavor chemical potential, could also be of relevance to other systems with phases (or phase transitions) which have been proposed to be described by (N≥2N\geq 2)-QED3  [35, 34, 75, 76, 77]. We are hopeful that our results are a key step toward establishing experimentally testable predictions that will eventually enable the identification of a fractionalized phase with deconfined gauge fields in a condensed matter system.

Note added.— Recently, Ref. [78] appeared, which considers symmetry breaking in QED3 in a mean background gauge flux (without an externally imposed Zeeman field) and is in agreement with our conclusions in Secs. II.3.1 and II.3.2 where results overlap. Further, Refs. [79, 80] also appeared recently, which study field-induced phases of frustrated triangular-lattice quantum antiferromagnets, to which our results may be applicable. In a similar vein, Ref. 65 studies Gutzwiller-projected finite-flux wave functions for triangular-lattice quantum antiferromagnets. We also note recent progress in hybrid Monte Carlo simulations of the lattice gauge theory (at zero Zeeman field) [64] closely related to the current investigation.

Data availability

Selected numerical data used to generate the figures are publicly available in the authors’ GitHub data repository [81]. The complete bin-resolved DQMC outputs and the original imaginary-time correlation functions used for SAC are available from the authors upon reasonable request because of their volume. The DQMC code is not publicly available.

Supplemental Material for
“Emergent Gauge Flux in Mixed QED3 with Flavor Chemical Potential:
Implications for Magnetized U(1) Dirac Spin Liquids”

The Supplemental Material provides details both in analytic derivations and quantum Monte Carlo simulations, as well as the benchmark data that are referred to in the main text.

I Lattice mean field magnetic spectra calculation

The formalism of the calculation has been applied in Ref. [49] for the π\pi-flux Hubbard model on the square lattice under the Zeeman field. We have employed GPU computation to accelerate the evaluation of the transverse and longitudinal spin susceptibilities, which enables access to larger lattice sizes with LL upto 60.

Let’s first look at the transverse channel. Start from real space and Matsubara frequency

χ±​(i,j,i​ωn)\displaystyle\chi^{\pm}(i,j,i\omega_{n}) =∑i​νnG↑​(j,i,i​νn)​G↓​(i,j,i​νn+i​ωn)\displaystyle=\sum_{i\nu_{n}}G_{\uparrow}\left(j,i,i\nu_{n}\right)G_{\downarrow}\left(i,j,i\nu_{n}+i\omega_{n}\right)
=∑i​νn(1(i​νn+μ)​𝕀N×N−H)j​i⋅(1(i​νn+i​ωn−μ)​𝕀N×N−H)i​j\displaystyle=\sum_{i\nu_{n}}\left(\frac{1}{(i\nu_{n}+\mu)\mathbb{I}_{N\times N}-H}\right)_{ji}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{(i\nu_{n}+i\omega_{n}-\mu)\mathbb{I}_{N\times N}-H}\right)_{ij}
=∑i​νn∑m∑lUj​m​1i​νn+μ−Dm​Um​i−1⋅Ui​l​1i​νn+i​ωn−μ−Dl​Ul​j−1\displaystyle=\sum_{i\nu_{n}}\sum_{m}\sum_{l}U_{jm}\frac{1}{i\nu_{n}+\mu-D_{m}}U_{mi}^{-1}\cdot U_{il}\frac{1}{i\nu_{n}+i\omega_{n}-\mu-D_{l}}U_{lj}^{-1}
=∑m∑lUj​m​Um​i−1​Ui​l​Ul​j−1​nF​(Dm−μ)−nF​(Dl+μ)i​ωn+Dm−Dl−2​μ\displaystyle=\sum_{m}\sum_{l}U_{jm}U_{mi}^{-1}U_{il}U_{lj}^{-1}\frac{n_{F}(D_{m}-\mu)-n_{F}(D_{l}+\mu)}{i\omega_{n}+D_{m}-D_{l}-2\mu} (S1)

where the singular value decomposition of the non-interacting (J=0)(J=0) Hamiltonian HH at μ=12​B\mu=\frac{1}{2}B is performed. After analytical continuation i​ωn→ω+i​η+i\omega_{n}\rightarrow\omega+i\eta^{+}, one has

χ±​(i,j,ω)=∑m∑lUj​m​Um​i−1​Ui​l​Ul​j−1​nF​(Dm−μ)−nF​(Dl+μ)ω+i​η++Dm−Dl−2​μ,\chi^{\pm}(i,j,\omega)=\sum_{m}\sum_{l}U_{jm}U_{mi}^{-1}U_{il}U_{lj}^{-1}\frac{n_{F}(D_{m}-\mu)-n_{F}(D_{l}+\mu)}{\omega+i\eta^{+}+D_{m}-D_{l}-2\mu}, (S2)

then we perform Fourier transformation to obtain momentum space dynamical susceptibility

χ±(q,ω)=1N∑i​jχ±(i,j,ω)⋅e−iq⋅ri​j,\displaystyle\chi^{\pm}(q,\omega)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{ij}\chi^{\pm}(i,j,\omega)\cdot e^{-iq\cdot r_{ij}}, (S3)

and the spectra is −2​Im​χ±​(q,ω)-2\text{Im}\chi^{\pm}(q,\omega).

In the actually lattice model computation, we can further analyze the formula to make it suitable for GPU simulation to access larger system sizes in shorter time

χ±​(q,ω)\displaystyle\chi^{\pm}(q,\omega) =1N∑i​jχ±(i,j,ω)⋅e−iq⋅ri​j\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{ij}\chi^{\pm}(i,j,\omega)\cdot e^{-iq\cdot r_{ij}}
=1N∑i​j∑m∑lUj​mUm​i−1Ui​lUl​j−1nF​(Dm−μ)−nF​(Dl+μ)ω+i​η++Dm−Dl−2​μ⋅e−iq⋅ri​j\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{ij}\sum_{m}\sum_{l}U_{jm}U_{mi}^{-1}U_{il}U_{lj}^{-1}\frac{n_{F}(D_{m}-\mu)-n_{F}(D_{l}+\mu)}{\omega+i\eta^{+}+D_{m}-D_{l}-2\mu}\cdot e^{-iq\cdot r_{ij}}
=∑m∑l[1N∑iUi​m∗Ui​le−iq⋅ri∑jUj​l∗Uj​me+iq⋅rj(nF(Dm−μ)−nF(Dl+μ))]1ω+i​η++Dm−Dl−2​μ\displaystyle=\sum_{m}\sum_{l}\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}U_{im}^{*}U_{il}e^{-iq\cdot r_{i}}\sum_{j}U_{jl}^{*}U_{jm}e^{+iq\cdot r_{j}}(n_{F}(D_{m}-\mu)-n_{F}(D_{l}+\mu))\right]\frac{1}{\omega+i\eta^{+}+D_{m}-D_{l}-2\mu}
=∑m​lΓ⁡(m,l,q)​G​(m,l,ω)\displaystyle=\sum_{ml}\Gamma(m,l,q)G(m,l,\omega) (S4)

One notices the matrix size of Γ⁡(m,l,q)\Gamma(m,l,q) is L2⋅L2⋅32​LL^{2}\cdot L^{2}\cdot\frac{3}{2}L and computation of each element involves sum over i,ji,j, which is perfect for GPU parallelization. The sum over m,lm,l for each (𝐪,ω)(\mathbf{q},\omega) is also well-suited for GPU parallelization. It is in such arrangement that the 60×6060\times 60 mean-field spectra in the Figs. 7, 8 and 9 of the main text are obtained.

In order to compute χ∓​(q,ω)\chi^{\mp}(q,\omega), we starts from χ∓​(i,j,i​ωn)=∑i​νnG↓​(j,i,i​νn)​G↑​(i,j,i​νn+i​ωn)\chi^{\mp}(i,j,i\omega_{n})=\sum_{i\nu_{n}}G_{\downarrow}(j,i,i\nu_{n})G_{\uparrow}(i,j,i\nu_{n}+i\omega_{n}) and in practice just need to replace μ→−μ\mu\rightarrow-\mu in the expression of Eq. (S4),

χ∓​(i,j,ω)\displaystyle\chi^{\mp}(i,j,\omega) =∑m∑lUj​m​Um​i−1​Ui​l​Ul​j−1​nF​(Dm+μ)−nF​(Dl−μ)ω+i​η++Dm−Dl+2​μ.\displaystyle=\sum_{m}\sum_{l}U_{jm}U_{mi}^{-1}U_{il}U_{lj}^{-1}\frac{n_{F}(D_{m}+\mu)-n_{F}(D_{l}-\mu)}{\omega+i\eta^{+}+D_{m}-D_{l}+2\mu}. (S5)

For χz​z​(q,ω)\chi^{zz}(q,\omega), it is

χz​z​(i,j,ω)=∑m∑lUj​m​Um​i−1​Ui​l​Ul​j−1​nF​(Dm−μ)−nF​(Dl−μ)+nF​(Dm+μ)−nF​(Dl+μ)ω+i​η++Dm−Dl.\displaystyle\chi^{zz}(i,j,\omega)=\sum_{m}\sum_{l}U_{jm}U_{mi}^{-1}U_{il}U_{lj}^{-1}\frac{n_{F}(D_{m}-\mu)-n_{F}(D_{l}-\mu)+n_{F}(D_{m}+\mu)-n_{F}(D_{l}+\mu)}{\omega+i\eta^{+}+D_{m}-D_{l}}. (S6)

Correspondingly, we follow the practice in Eq. (S4) to modify Γ⁡(m,l,q)\Gamma(m,l,q) and G⁡(m,l,ω)G(m,l,\omega) and GPU compute χ∓​(q,ω)\chi^{\mp}(q,\omega) and χz​z​(q,ω)\chi^{zz}(q,\omega) accordingly.

II Dynamical spin spectra from low-energy field theory

A continuum field theory approach is applicable at high-symmetry points 𝚪,𝑿,𝑴\bm{\Gamma},\bm{X},\bm{M} where the zero-field U(1) Dirac spin liquid features a gapless dynamical spin susceptibility arising from intra/inter-valley particle-hole excitations of Dirac fermions.

In the presence of a finite emergent gauge flux, the spinons are confined to relativistic Landau levels. We find the corresponding spin susceptibility by first deriving the propagator for Dirac fermions in relativistic Landau levels, and then subsequently calculate the dynamical response function as a fermionic bubble diagram.

II.1 Propagator

We first derive the propagator for Dirac fermions coupled to the emergent gauge field aa with a non-zero internal gauge flux. Picking a Landau gauge a=ϕ​x​y^a=\phi x\hat{y}, we take the Hamiltonian for the α=↑(+1),↓(−1)\alpha=\uparrow(+1),\downarrow(-1) spinons (suppressing all indices) as

Hσ=v​∫d2​𝒙​ψ†​(x,y,t)​[γx​px+γy​(py−Ay)−b​α2]​ψ​(x,y,t).H_{\sigma}=v\int\mathrm{d}^{2}\bm{x}\,\psi^{\dagger}(x,y,t)\left[\gamma^{x}p_{x}+\gamma^{y}(p_{y}-A_{y})-b\frac{\alpha}{2}\right]\psi(x,y,t). (S7)

The solutions to the Dirac equation with energy ±En=±v2​n/ℓ\pm E_{n}=\pm v\sqrt{2n}/\ell are then of the form φpy,±(n)​(𝒙,t)=ei​py​y​12​(φn,±φn−1)\varphi_{p_{y},\pm}^{(n)}(\bm{x},t)=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}p_{y}y}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\varphi_{n},\pm\varphi_{n-1}) with φn=12n​n!​π​ℓe−(x/ℓ−pyℓ)2/2Hn(x/ℓ−pyℓ)\varphi_{n}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n}n!\sqrt{\pi}\ell}}\mathrm{e}^{-(x/\ell-p_{y}\ell)^{2}/2}H_{n}(x/\ell-p_{y}\ell) with Hermite polynomials HnH_{n}, and ϕn=−1≡0\phi_{n=-1}\equiv 0. We henceforth take v=1v=1 for simplicity.

From this, we obtain the propagator GA​B=⟨0|ΨA​(x)​ΨB†​(x′)|0⟩G_{AB}=\braket{0|\Psi_{A}(x)\Psi_{B}^{\dagger}(x^{\prime})|0} (in imaginary time) via a mode-expansion (alternatively, functional methods may be used) as

Gα(x,x′)=e−ξ/2ei​Φ​(x,x′)2​π​ℓ2∫d​ω2​πe−i​ω​(t−t′)[𝒫+i​ω+α​b/2+∑n=1∞{(i​ω+α​b/2)​(𝒫+​Ln0​(ξ)+𝒫−​Ln−10​(ξ))(i​ω+α​b/2)2−En2+i​𝜸⋅(𝒙−𝒙′)​Ln−11​(ξ)/ℓ2(i​ω+α​b/2)2−En2]},G^{\alpha}(x,x^{\prime})=\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-\xi/2}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Phi(x,x^{\prime})}}{2\pi\ell^{2}}\int\frac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{2\pi}\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\omega(t-t^{\prime})}\Big[\frac{\mathcal{P}_{+}}{\mathrm{i}\omega+\alpha b/2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\Big\{\frac{(\mathrm{i}\omega+\alpha b/2)(\mathcal{P}_{+}L_{n}^{0}(\xi)+\mathcal{P}_{-}L_{n-1}^{0}(\xi))}{(\mathrm{i}\omega+\alpha b/2)^{2}-E_{n}^{2}}\\ +\frac{\mathrm{i}\bm{\gamma}\cdot(\bm{x}-\bm{x}^{\prime})L^{1}_{n-1}(\xi)/\ell^{2}}{(\mathrm{i}\omega+\alpha b/2)^{2}-E_{n}^{2}}\Big]\Big\}, (S8)

where we use that GA​BG_{AB} is spin-diagonal to explicitly label the α=↑,↓\alpha=\uparrow,\downarrow components, and make all other indices implicit (via matrix notation). Here, Lnm​(x)L^{m}_{n}(x) are Laguerre polynomials that arise from using the identity

∫−∞∞d​x​e−x2​Hm​(x+y)​Hn​(x+z)=2n​π​m!​zn−m​Lmn−m​(−2​y​z)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{e}^{-x^{2}}H_{m}(x+y)H_{n}(x+z)=2^{n}\sqrt{\pi}m!z^{n-m}L^{n-m}_{m}(-2yz) (S9)

and the Schwinger phase is given by Φ⁡(𝒙,𝒙′)=(x+x′)​(y−y′)/(2​ℓ2)\Phi(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})=(x+x^{\prime})(y-y^{\prime})/(2\ell^{2}), and ξ=ξ⁡(𝒙,𝒙′)=((x−x′)2+(y−y′)2)/(2​ℓ2)\xi=\xi(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})=\left((x-x^{\prime})^{2}+(y-y^{\prime})^{2}\right)/(2\ell^{2}).

II.2 Magnetization

For consistency, we can compute the uniform magnetization from the propagator (in imaginary time) as mz=12​⟨ψ†​(t+ϵ,x)​σz​ψ​(t,x)⟩m^{z}=\frac{1}{2}\langle\psi^{\dagger}(t+\epsilon,x)\sigma^{z}\psi(t,x)\rangle with ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Noting that Φ⁡(𝒙,𝒙)=0\Phi(\bm{x},\bm{x})=0 and ξ⁡(𝒙,𝒙)=0\xi(\bm{x},\bm{x})=0, and using tr⁡𝒫±=1\tr\mathcal{P}_{\pm}=1 as well as Ln0​(0)=1L^{0}_{n}(0)=1, we find

mLLz=12​tr⁡[G+​(x,t,x,t+ϵ)−G−​(x,t,x,t+ϵ)]=12​π​ℓ2​[(1+∑n=1∞1)−(∑n=1∞1)]=12​π​ℓ2=Φ2​π.m^{z}_{\mathrm{LL}}=\frac{1}{2}\tr[G^{+}(x,t;x,t+\epsilon)-G^{-}(x,t;x,t+\epsilon)]=\frac{1}{2\pi\ell^{2}}\left[\left(1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1\right)-\left(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1\right)\right]=\frac{1}{2\pi\ell^{2}}=\frac{\Phi}{2\pi}. (S10)

II.3 Susceptibility bubble diagram

By tracing how lattice-scale symmetry operations act on the low-energy spinon degrees of freedom, we obtain field-theory expressions for microscopic spin operators at the 𝚪\bm{\Gamma}, 𝑴\bm{M} and 𝑿\bm{X}-points as

S𝚪α\displaystyle S^{\alpha}_{\bm{\Gamma}} ∼12​Ψ¯​γ0​σα​Ψ\displaystyle\sim\frac{1}{2}\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{0}\sigma^{\alpha}\Psi (S11a)
S𝑴α\displaystyle S^{\alpha}_{\bm{M}} ∼12​ψ¯​σa​μx​ψ\displaystyle\sim\frac{1}{2}\bar{\psi}\sigma^{a}\mu^{x}\psi (S11b)
S𝑿α\displaystyle S^{\alpha}_{\bm{X}} ∼12​ψ¯​σa​μz​…​ψ\displaystyle\sim\frac{1}{2}\bar{\psi}\sigma^{a}\mu^{z}\dots\psi (S11c)

With this identification, we obtain dynamical susceptibilities in imaginary time as

χA​B(iν,𝒌)∼V−1∫dtei​ν​t∫d2𝒙d2𝒙′e−i𝐤⋅(𝒙−𝒙′)tr(γσμ)AG(t,𝒙;0,𝒙′)(γσμ)BG(0,𝒙′;t,𝒙),\chi^{AB}(\mathrm{i}\nu,\bm{k})\sim V^{-1}\int\mathrm{d}t\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\nu t}\int\mathrm{d}^{2}\bm{x}\mathrm{d}^{2}\bm{x}^{\prime}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}{\mathbf{k}}\cdot(\bm{x}-\bm{x}^{\prime})}\tr(\gamma\sigma\mu)^{A}G(t,\bm{x};0,\bm{x}^{\prime})(\gamma\sigma\mu)^{B}G(0,\bm{x}^{\prime};t,\bm{x}), (S12)

where A,BA,B are composite indices that are determined by choosing the respective vertices according to Eqs. (S11a)-(S11c). Using ξ⁡(𝒙,𝒙′)=ξ⁡(𝒙′,𝒙)\xi(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})=\xi(\bm{x}^{\prime},\bm{x}) and Φ⁡(𝒙,𝒙′)=−Φ⁡(𝒙′,𝒙)\Phi(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})=-\Phi(\bm{x}^{\prime},\bm{x}) so that the Schwinger phases in the propagators cancel, one can integrate over the center-of-mass coordinate 𝑹=(𝒙+𝒙′)/2\bm{R}=(\bm{x}+\bm{x}^{\prime})/2. The subsequent integrals over the relative spatial coordinate 𝒓=𝒙−𝒙′\bm{r}=\bm{x}-\bm{x}^{\prime} can be done in polar coordinates, where the angular integral gives rise to Bessel functions of the first kind. The remaining radial integrals over products of Bessel functions with Laguerre polynomials can be reduced to tabulated integrals (see Chapter 7 in Ref. [37]). We then arrive at

χ+⁣−𝚪(iν,𝒌)=−2×e−|𝒌|2ℓ2/22​π​ℓ2[1i​ν−b+∑n=1∞1n!(ℓ2​|𝒌|22)n1i​ν−b−En+12∑n=1,m=1∞(−1)n+m(i​ν−b)2−(Em+En)2×{(Em+En)(ℒn,m0,0(ℓ2|𝒌|2/2)+ℒn,m1,1(ℓ2|𝒌|2/2))−Em+EnEm​En4​nℓ2ℒn,m0,1(ℓ2𝒌2)}],\chi^{+-}_{\bm{\Gamma}}(\mathrm{i}\nu,\bm{k})=-2\times\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-|\bm{k}|^{2}\ell^{2}/2}}{2\pi\ell^{2}}\bigg[\frac{1}{\mathrm{i}\nu-b}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\left(\frac{\ell^{2}|\bm{k}|^{2}}{2}\right)^{n}\frac{1}{\mathrm{i}\nu-b-E_{n}}\\ +\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1,m=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+m}}{(\mathrm{i}\nu-b)^{2}-(E_{m}+E_{n})^{2}}\times\big\{(E_{m}+E_{n})\left(\mathcal{L}^{n,m}_{0,0}(\ell^{2}|\bm{k}|^{2}/2)+\mathcal{L}^{n,m}_{1,1}(\ell^{2}|\bm{k}|^{2}/2)\right)\\ -\frac{E_{m}+E_{n}}{E_{m}E_{n}}\frac{4n}{\ell^{2}}\mathcal{L}^{n,m}_{0,1}(\ell^{2}\bm{k}^{2})\big\}\bigg], (S13)

where we use the notation ℒs,rn,m​(x)=Ln−sm−n​(x)​Lm−rn−m​(x)\mathcal{L}^{n,m}_{s,r}(x)=L^{m-n}_{n-s}(x)L^{n-m}_{m-r}(x) for products of Laguerre polynomials.

The structure factor S𝚪+⁣−​(ω,q)S^{+-}_{\bm{\Gamma}}(\omega,q) can now be obtained from (S13) via the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, S𝚪+⁣−​(ω,q)=−2​Θ​(ω)​χ+⁣−′′​(ω,q)S^{+-}_{\bm{\Gamma}}(\omega,q)=-2\Theta(\omega)\chi^{\prime\prime}_{+-}(\omega,q) where χ+⁣−′′(ω,q)=ℑ[χ𝚪+⁣−(iω→ω+i0+,q)]\chi^{\prime\prime}_{+-}(\omega,q)=\Im[\chi^{+-}_{\bm{\Gamma}}(\mathrm{i}\omega\to\omega+\mathrm{i}0^{+},q)].

To compute S−⁣+​(ω,q)S^{-+}(\omega,q), we use the KMS condition to write S−⁣+​(ω,q)=eβ​ω​S+⁣−​(−ω,q)S^{-+}(\omega,q)=\mathrm{e}^{\beta\omega}S^{+-}(-\omega,q). Then, using the fluctuation-dissipation theorem and letting β→∞\beta\to\infty, we have eβ​ωS+⁣−(−ω,q)=eβ​ω2(1+n(−ω))χ+⁣−′′(−ω,q)≡−2θ(ω)χ+⁣−′′(−ω,q)\mathrm{e}^{\beta\omega}S^{+-}(-\omega,q)=\mathrm{e}^{\beta\omega}2(1+n(-\omega))\chi^{{}^{\prime\prime}}_{+-}(-\omega,q)\equiv-2\theta(\omega)\chi^{\prime\prime}_{+-}(-\omega,q) (note that Eq. (S13) is even under q→−qq\to-q). Here, we see that finite contributions to S−⁣+​(ω,q)S^{-+}(\omega,q) only arise from negative-frequency poles in the analytically continued Eq. (S13). These occur only in the last term of Eq. (S13), and thus at frequencies ω=−(Em+En)+b\omega=-(E_{m}+E_{n})+b, where m,n≥1m,n\geq 1.

II.4 Dispersion of poles

To find the dispersion relation of poles for small |𝒌||\bm{k}| away from the Γ\Gamma-point, we focus for simplicity only on the contribution to the analytically continued expression of Eq. (S13) and find the maximum spectral weight as a function of k=|𝒌|k=|\bm{k}|:

0​=!​∂∂k​[e−k2​ℓ22​1n!​(ℓ2​k22)n],0\overset{!}{=}\frac{\partial}{\partial k}\left[\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{k^{2}\ell^{2}}{2}}\frac{1}{n!}\left(\frac{\ell^{2}k^{2}}{2}\right)^{n}\right], (S14)

which yields ℓ2​kmax2=2​n\ell^{2}k^{2}_{\mathrm{max}}=2n. We plug this into the pole ν=En+b\nu=E_{n}+b by using that En=2​n/ℓE_{n}=\sqrt{2n}/\ell, yielding the dispersion relation for the maximum spectral weight located at the poles as

νmax​(|𝒌|)=|𝒌|+b.\nu_{\mathrm{max}}(|\bm{k}|)=|\bm{k}|+b. (S15)

Such behavior is shown in Fig. 6 in the main text.

III Larmor’s theorem and sum rules

Considering the correlation function S+⁣−​(t)=⟨S+​(t)​S−​(0)⟩S^{+-}(t)=\langle S^{+}(t)S^{-}(0)\rangle and S−⁣+​(t)=⟨S−​(t)​S+​(0)⟩S^{-+}(t)=\langle S^{-}(t)S^{+}(0)\rangle, we note that [S+,S−]=2​Sz[S^{+},S^{-}]=2S^{z} implies for their Fourier transforms ∫d​ω2​π​(S+⁣−​(ω)−S−⁣+​(ω))=2​⟨Sz⟩\int\frac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{2\pi}\left(S^{+-}(\omega)-S^{-+}(\omega)\right)=2\langle S^{z}\rangle. Using the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, the integrand can be expressed in terms of the imaginary part of the corresponding susceptibility, S+⁣−(ω)−S−⁣+(ω)=2Θ(ω)(χ(ω)+⁣−′′−χ(−ω)+⁣−′′)S^{+-}(\omega)-S^{-+}(\omega)=2\Theta(\omega)(\chi{{}^{\prime\prime}}_{+-}(\omega)-\chi{{}^{\prime\prime}}_{+-}(-\omega)). We thus obtain the sum rule

∫−∞∞d​ω2​π​χ+⁣−′′​(ω)=⟨Sz⟩.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{2\pi}\chi^{\prime\prime}_{+-}(\omega)=\langle S^{z}\rangle. (S16)

Larmor’s theorem [47, 49] then implies, upon identifying 𝐒{\mathbf{S}} with the system’s total spin, i.e. considering correlation functions at the 𝚪\bm{\Gamma}-point, the dynamical susceptibility must thus be of the form

χ+⁣−′′​(ω)=2​π​mz​δ​(ω−b)\chi_{+-}^{\prime\prime}(\omega)=2\pi m^{z}\delta(\omega-b) (S17)

This also implies (at zero temperature, for b>0b>0) that the structure factor S𝚪+⁣−​(ω)=2​(2​π​mz)​δ​(ω−b)S^{+-}_{\bm{\Gamma}}(\omega)=2(2\pi m^{z})\delta(\omega-b) while S𝚪−⁣+​(ω)≡0S^{-+}_{\bm{\Gamma}}(\omega)\equiv 0.

As a cross-check, we now show that χ𝚪+⁣−​(i​ν,𝒌)\chi_{\bm{\Gamma}}^{+-}(\mathrm{i}\nu,\bm{k}) as given in Eq. (S13) satisfies Larmor’s theorem. To this end, note that the second term in Eq. (S13) vanishes as 𝒌→0\bm{k}\to 0. For the last term, use that

Ln−1m−n​(0)​Lm−1n−m​(0)=(n−1+m−nn−1)​(m−1+n−mm−1)≡δn,m,L^{m-n}_{n-1}(0)L^{n-m}_{m-1}(0)=\tbinom{n-1+m-n}{n-1}\tbinom{m-1+n-m}{m-1}\equiv\delta_{n,m}, (S18)

and further also

Lnm−n​(0)​Lm−1n−m​(0)=(n+m−nn)​(m−1+n−mm−1)≡δn,m.L^{m-n}_{n}(0)L^{n-m}_{m-1}(0)=\tbinom{n+m-n}{n}\tbinom{m-1+n-m}{m-1}\equiv\delta_{n,m}. (S19)

So the Laguerre-polynomials in Eq. (S13) at 𝒌=0\bm{k}=0 just give δn,m\delta_{n,m}, and we can cancel the mm-summation and get a single sum over nn. The brace then becomes (observe that 2​n​ℓ−2≡En22n\ell^{-2}\equiv E_{n}^{2}):

∑n,m=1∞(…)​δn,m​{2​(Em+En)−Em+EnEm​En​4​nℓ2}=∑n=1∞{4​En−2​EnEn2​En2×2}≡0.\sum_{n,m=1}^{\infty}(\dots)\delta_{n,m}\big\{2(E_{m}+E_{n})-\frac{E_{m}+E_{n}}{E_{m}E_{n}}\frac{4n}{\ell^{2}}\big\}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left\{4E_{n}-\frac{2E_{n}}{E_{n}^{2}}E_{n}^{2}\times 2\right\}\equiv 0. (S20)

So at 𝒌=0\bm{k}=0, the dynamical response is given by

χ+⁣−(iν,k)∼−2×12​π​ℓ21i​ν−b\chi^{+-}(\mathrm{i}\nu,{k})\sim-2\times\frac{1}{2\pi\ell^{2}}\frac{1}{\mathrm{i}\nu-b} (S21)

Analytic continuation then yields χ+⁣−′′​(ω,0)=1ℓ2​δ​(ω−b)\chi^{\prime\prime}_{+-}(\omega,0)=\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}\delta(\omega-b), which is in agreement with Eq. (S17) upon identifying mz=1/(2​π​ℓ2)m^{z}=1/(2\pi\ell^{2}), which is precisely the magnetization of the state under consideration (see Eq. (S10)).

In Figs. 6 and 7(a) and (c), the Larmor mode at Γ\Gamma in the transverse magnetic spectra is clearly seen in both field-theoretical calculations and lattice-model (mean-field and QMC) simulations. It has also been previously observed in QMC simulations of magnetized Dirac fermions in a Hubbard-model setting [49].

IV Analysis of flux-flux correlation functions

IV.1 Free photon theory (non-compact 2+1-dim. electrodynamics without fermions)

In this section, we consider a free photon theory and analyze the fluctuation of the magnetic flux, which arises from the Goldstone mode of a spontaneously broken U(1)m symmetry. The Lagrangian of the free photon theory is a non-compact QED3:

L=∑r12​J​∑a=x,y[aα​(x,y,τ+eτ)−aα​(x,y,τ)|eτ|]2+∑rK2​[ax​(r)+ay​(r+ex)−ax​(r+ey)−ay​(r)]2,L=\sum_{r}\frac{1}{2J}\sum_{a=x,y}\left[\frac{a_{\alpha}\left(x,y,\tau+e_{\tau}\right)-a_{\alpha}(x,y,\tau)}{\left|e_{\tau}\right|}\right]^{2}+\sum_{r}\frac{K}{2}\left[a_{x}(r)+a_{y}\left(r+e_{x}\right)-a_{x}\left(r+e_{y}\right)-a_{y}(r)\right]^{2}, (S22)

where aα​(r)a_{\alpha}(r) is the gauge field which lives on a bond with direction α∈{x,y}\alpha\in\{x,y\}, whose left or bottom end point is on the site r=(x,y,τ)r=(x,y,\tau). The KK term consists of magnetic flux defined as Φ⁡(r)=∇×aα​(r)=ax​(r)+ay​(r+ex)−ax​(r+ey)−ay​(r)\Phi(r)=\nabla\times a_{\alpha}(r)=a_{x}(r)+a_{y}\left(r+e_{x}\right)-a_{x}\left(r+e_{y}\right)-a_{y}(r), which goes through a spatial plaquette whose bottom left corner is at site rr. We have also chosen the τ\tau unit cell |eτ|=1/J|e_{\tau}|=1/J. Transforming the Lagrangian to the kk-space, we can obtain the flux correlation function

⟨Φ⁡(r)​Φ​(0)⟩=1V​∑kx,ky,ωnei​kx​x+i​ky​y+i​ωn​τ​2​(cos⁡[kx]+cos⁡[ky]−2)cos⁡[ωn]−1+K/J⋅(cos⁡[kx]+cos⁡[ky]−2).\left\langle\Phi(r)\Phi\left(0\right)\right\rangle=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{k_{x},k_{y},\omega_{n}}\!\!e^{ik_{x}x+ik_{y}y+i\omega_{n}\tau}\frac{2\left(\cos\left[k_{x}\right]+\cos\left[k_{y}\right]-2\right)}{\cos\left[\omega_{n}\right]-1+K/J\cdot\left(\cos\left[k_{x}\right]+\cos\left[k_{y}\right]-2\right)}. (S23)

The imaginary-time flux correlation function ⟨Φ⁡(x,y,τ)​Φ​(x,y,0)⟩\left\langle\Phi(x,y,\tau)\,\Phi(x,y,0)\right\rangle is plotted in Fig. S1. The fit line is y=0.12/(τ3+0.2)y=0.12/(\tau^{3}+0.2) which agrees with 1/τ31/\tau^{3} scaling behavior in the low-frequency limit (large τ\tau) obtained from the analytical expression above, which is a consequence of gapless spectrum of the gauge field.

IV.2 Mixed QED3 (with fermionic matter)

We also investigate the scaling of dynamical flux correlation for mixed QED3 with fermion coupling. The results are shown in Fig. S2. DSL phase with Dirac-type gapless spinon dispersion shows Cχ​(τ)∼τ−4C_{\chi}(\tau)\sim\tau^{-4} asymptotic scaling behavior at large τ\tau, while at B=3B=3, the deconfined AFM with gapped fermion shows better agreement with a Cχ​(τ)∼τ−3C_{\chi}(\tau)\sim\tau^{-3} asymptotic behavior at large τ\tau. An unambiguous power-law exponent is difficult to extract from these results, due to the challenge of avoiding non-universal short-time features at small τ\tau and finite-size cutoffs at large τ\tau of order β\beta. Nevertheless, we see that the theoretically predicted scalings (Sec. IIC3) are at least consistent with the data in a range of intermediate τ\tau. In order to study the variation of the fitted power α\alpha in C⁡(τ)∼A​τ−αC(\tau)\sim A\tau^{-\alpha} versus the fitting window, we perform the fitting starting from τ=0\tau=0 to τ=β/2\tau=\beta/2 with fitting window Δ​τ=1\Delta\tau=1 and show the results in Fig. S2(b). We observe that the fitted power α\alpha at small τ\tau and τ∼β/2\tau\sim\beta/2 deviate from α∼4\alpha\sim 4 for DSL and α∼3\alpha\sim 3 for AFM. In order to study the asymptotic behavior, we need to use larger τ\tau but eventually stopped by large numerical error before reaching τ∼β/2\tau\sim\beta/2.

V zz-direction flux insertion and global update

In DQMC simulations, one can introduce zz-direction flux into the model. The consequence is shifted momentum points in Brillouin zone, thus offering extra momentum points otherwise unavailable for that system size. Finite size effects can be effectively reduced with this method [42, 43]. The flux is introduced via Peierls phase factors with aoa_{o} the orbital phase factor, 𝐀o​(𝐫){\mathbf{A}}_{o}({\mathbf{r}}) the vector potential and Φ0\Phi_{0} the flux quanta. In Landau gauge, we choose 𝐀o​(𝐫)=−Bo​(y,0,0){\mathbf{A}}_{o}({\mathbf{r}})=-B_{o}(y,0,0) with BoB_{o} the introduced orbital magnetic field. In order to respect periodic boundary condition, we use a gauge transformation for the vector potential on the boundary

𝐀o​(𝐫+L​𝐞x)\displaystyle{\mathbf{A}}_{o}({\mathbf{r}}+L{\mathbf{e}}_{x}) =𝐀o​(𝐫)+∇χx​(𝐫)\displaystyle={\mathbf{A}}_{o}({\mathbf{r}})+{\mathbf{\nabla}}\chi_{x}({\mathbf{r}})
𝐀o​(𝐫+L​𝐞y)\displaystyle{\mathbf{A}}_{o}({\mathbf{r}}+L{\mathbf{e}}_{y}) =𝐀o​(𝐫)+∇χy​(𝐫)\displaystyle={\mathbf{A}}_{o}({\mathbf{r}})+{\mathbf{\nabla}}\chi_{y}({\mathbf{r}}) (S24)

and the corresponding boundary condition for fermion

ψ¯𝐢+L​𝐞x\displaystyle\bar{\psi}_{{\mathbf{i}}+L{\mathbf{e}}_{x}} =e2​π​iΦ0​χx​(𝐢)​ψ¯𝐢\displaystyle=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{\Phi_{0}}\chi_{x}({\mathbf{i}})}\bar{\psi}_{{\mathbf{i}}}
ψ𝐢+L​𝐞y\displaystyle\psi_{{\mathbf{i}}+L{\mathbf{e}}_{y}} =e2​π​iΦ0​χy​(𝐢)​ψ𝐢\displaystyle=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{\Phi_{0}}\chi_{y}({\mathbf{i}})}\psi_{{\mathbf{i}}} (S25)

We choose χx​(𝐢)=0\chi_{x}({{\mathbf{i}}})=0 and χy​(𝐢)=−Bo​L​x\chi_{y}({{\mathbf{i}}})=-B_{o}Lx with orbital magnetic field satisfying

Bo⋅L2Φ0=NΦ\frac{B_{o}\cdot L^{2}}{\Phi_{0}}=N_{\Phi} (S26)

with NΦN_{\Phi} an integer to ensure uniqueness of wave function. In conclusion, ao,x=−2​π​NΦ​yL2a_{o,x}=-\frac{2\pi N_{\Phi}y}{L^{2}}, ao,y=0a_{o,y}=0 away from boundary and ao,y=2​π​NΦ​xLa_{o,y}=\frac{2\pi N_{\Phi}x}{L} for boundary bonds.

Based on this method, we can propose global space-time gauge field update by inserting random NΦN_{\Phi} zz-direction flux uniformly for all imaginary time slices to the current gauge field configuration. It helps to quickly evolve to the desired flux sector and traditional local update will explore the whole phase space ergodically. As mentioned in Sec. IIB in the main text, we combine both the global and the local updates in the QMC sampling process.

VI U(1)m symmetry and duality map

The action in Eq. (1) of the main text is of a “mixed” compact/non-compact character: on the one hand, the coupling between gauge field and fermions suggests ai​j​(τn)∼ai​j​(τn)+2​πa_{ij}(\tau_{n})\sim a_{ij}(\tau_{n})+2\pi, as common in compact U(1) lattice gauge theories. On the other hand, the kinetic term of the gauge field, which couples the gauge field between different time slices, spoils such a putative compactness in the time-continuum limit. This unusual behaviour is distinct from fully compact or non-compact theories, and is the motivation behind the nomenclature of “mixed” QED3 in the main text.

In order to gain insight into the properties of a theory which is periodic in the gauge-field along certain space-time directions only, we consider a simplified effective pure gauge theory model. Such a theory will capture the low-energy dynamics in phases where the fermions have a finite gap and can be integrated out.

VI.1 Effective action for gapped states

Integrating-out the fermionic degrees of freedom will give rise to terms periodic in the field strength on spatial plaquettes (i.e. plaquettes at constant τ\tau), while the temporal plaquettes feature a non-compact kinetic term for the gauge field,

S=−1gτ2∑rcos(ϵτ​i​jΔiAr,j)+12​g2∑r,i(ΔτAr,i−ΔiAr,τ)2,S=-\frac{1}{g_{\tau}^{2}}\sum_{r}\cos(\epsilon_{\tau ij}\Delta_{i}A_{r,j})+\frac{1}{2g^{2}}\sum_{r,i}(\Delta_{\tau}A_{r,i}-\Delta_{i}A_{r,\tau})^{2}, (S27)

with the associated partition function Z=∫ℝD⁡[A]​e−SZ=\int_{\mathbb{R}}D[A]e^{-S}. Here, rr are coordinates for the sites of the 2+1-dim. space-time lattice with unit vectors x^,y^,τ^\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{\tau} (latin indices are used for spatial components i=x,yi=x,y while τ\tau denotes the temporal component), and Δμ​fr=fr+μ^−fr\Delta_{\mu}f_{r}=f_{r+\hat{\mu}}-f_{r} denotes the forward difference operator (with μ=x,y,z\mu=x,y,z), i.e. a lattice discretization of the partial derivative ∂μ\partial_{\mu}. For later convenience, we have also explicitly kept the temporal component of the gauge field Ar,τA_{r,\tau}, while in Eq. (1) of the main text we are using the temporal gauge Ar,τ≡0A_{r,\tau}\equiv 0.

Making a Villain approximation of the cosine, et​cos⁡(x)≈∑k∈ℤe−t/2(x−2πk)2e^{t\cos(x)}\approx\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{-t/2(x-2\pi k)^{2}}, one obtains

S=12​gτ2​∑r(Δx​Ar,y−Δy​Ar,x−2​π​kr,τ)2+12​g2​∑r,i(Δτ​Ar,i−Δi​Ar,τ)2−∑rhr,τ(ΔxAr,y−ΔyAr,x−2πkr,τ)−∑r,i,jhr,i(ΔjAr,τ−ΔτAr,j)ϵi​j​τ.S=\frac{1}{2g_{\tau}^{2}}\sum_{r}\left(\Delta_{x}A_{r,y}-\Delta_{y}A_{r,x}-2\pi k_{r,\tau}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{2g^{2}}\sum_{r,i}(\Delta_{\tau}A_{r,i}-\Delta_{i}A_{r,\tau})^{2}\\ -\sum_{r}h_{r,\tau}\left(\Delta_{x}A_{r,y}-\Delta_{y}A_{r,x}-2\pi k_{r,\tau}\right)-\sum_{r,i,j}h_{r,i}(\Delta_{j}A_{r,\tau}-\Delta_{\tau}A_{r,j})\epsilon^{ij\tau}. (S28)

Here, for convenience, we have also introduced a three-component background field hr,μh_{r,\mu} that can be associated with a plaquette anchored at rr and normal vector μ\mu. The field hh may be used to compute expectation values on spatial and temporal plaquettes as

⟨sin⁡(Δx​Ar,y−Δy​Ar,x)⟩=δδ​hr,τ​log⁡Z⁡[h]|h=0and⟨Δj​Ar,τ−Δτ​Ar,j⟩​ϵi​j​τ=δδ​hr,i​log⁡Z⁡[h]|h=0.\langle\sin\left(\Delta_{x}A_{r,y}-\Delta_{y}A_{r,x}\right)\rangle=\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta h_{r,\tau}}\log Z[h]\right|_{h=0}\quad\text{and}\quad\langle\Delta_{j}A_{r,\tau}-\Delta_{\tau}A_{r,j}\rangle\epsilon^{ij\tau}=\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta h_{r,i}}\log Z[h]\right|_{h=0}. (S29)

The first equality is obtained from Eq. (S27), after consistently including the field hh therein. We emphasize that these (local) expectation values are to be taken with respect to the full action, and in particular include summing over all possible sectors of the integer variables kr,τk_{r,\tau}.

In a fixed sector defined by the Villain variables kr,τ∈ℤk_{r,\tau}\in\mathbb{Z}, the total flux through a time slice (spanned by sites with τ=const.\tau=\mathrm{const}.) is given by the sum F⁡(τn)=∑(rx,ry)F(rx,ry,τn),τF(\tau_{n})=\sum_{(r_{x},r_{y})}F_{(r_{x},r_{y},\tau_{n}),\tau}, where Fr,τF_{r,\tau} is obtained as a variation Fr,τ=δ/δ​hr,τ​(−S)|hr,τ=0=Δx​Ar,y−Δy​Ar,x−2​π​kr,τF_{r,\tau}=\left.\delta/\delta h_{r,\tau}(-S)\right|_{h_{r,\tau}=0}=\Delta_{x}A_{r,y}-\Delta_{y}A_{r,x}-2\pi k_{r,\tau}. With periodic boundary conditions, the smooth contributions cancel, and we find a quantized total flux through a given time slice, determined by the Villain variables as

F⁡(τn)=∑(rx,ry)(−2​π​k(rx,ry,τn),τ)∈2​π​ℤ.F(\tau_{n})=\sum_{(r_{x},r_{y})}(-2\pi k_{(r_{x},r_{y},\tau_{n}),\tau})\in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}. (S30)

VI.2 Duality mapping

Resumming the first term via ∑k∈ℤe−12​t​(x−2​π​k)2=t2​π​∑n∈ℤe−t2​n2+i​x​n\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{-\frac{1}{2t}(x-2\pi k)^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{t}{2\pi}}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{-\frac{t}{2}n^{2}+ixn}, dropping a term quadratic in the background field hh, and using a Hubbard-Stratonovich decoupling for the second set of terms yields the action (we neglect terms quadratic in hh)

S=∑r[gτ22(nr,τ)2+g22((br,y)2+(br,x)2)]−i∑r[nr,τ((ΔxAr,y−ΔyAr,x)−g2τhr,τ)−∑iϵi​j​τ((ΔjAr,τ−ΔτAr,j)−g2hr,i)br,i],S=\sum_{r}\left[\frac{g_{\tau}^{2}}{2}(n_{r,\tau})^{2}+\frac{g^{2}}{2}\left((b_{r,y})^{2}+(b_{r,x})^{2}\right)\right]-i\sum_{r}\Big[n_{r,\tau}((\Delta_{x}A_{r,y}-\Delta_{y}A_{r,x})-g^{2}_{\tau}h_{r,\tau})\\ -\sum_{i}\epsilon^{ij\tau}((\Delta_{j}A_{r,\tau}-\Delta_{\tau}A_{r,j})-g^{2}h_{r,i})b_{r,i}\Big], (S31)

and the partition function becomes Z=∑{n∈ℤ}∫ℝD[A]∫ℝD[b]e−SZ=\sum_{\{n\in\mathbb{Z}\}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}D[A]\int_{\mathbb{R}}D[b]e^{-S}. Here, the spatial components br,xb_{r,x} and br,yb_{r,y} are ℝ\mathbb{R}-valued, while the integer-valued nature of the temporal component nr,τ∈ℤn_{r,\tau}\in\mathbb{Z} directly follows from the fact that Eq. (S27) is periodic in the flux on spatial plaquettes.

For a unified treatment, we use the Poisson summation formula11 1 For some function f⁡(n)f(n) of integers, we may write ∑n∈ℤf⁡(n)=∫−∞∞d​ϕ​∑n∈ℤδ⁡(n−ϕ)​f​(ϕ)≡∫−∞∞d​ϕ​∑m∈ℤei​2​π​m​ϕ​f​(ϕ)\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f(n)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}{\mathrm{d}\phi}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\delta(n-\phi)f(\phi)\equiv\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}{\mathrm{d}\phi}\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{i2\pi m\phi}f(\phi). rewrite nr,τn_{r,\tau} in terms of a ℝ\mathbb{R}-valued field (which we can identify as the temporal component br,τb_{r,\tau} of a vector field br,μb_{r,\mu}) along with a quantization constraint. Further performing a partial resummation (i.e. the discrete version of partial integration), one then arrives at

S=∑r[gτ22​(br,τ)2+g22​((br,x)2+(br,y)2)]+i∑r[Ar,τ(Δ¯ybr,x−Δ¯xbr,y)+Ar,x(Δ¯τbr,y−Δ¯ybr,τ)+Ar,y(Δ¯xbr,τ−Δ¯τbr,x)]−2πi∑rmrbr,τ+ig2τ∑rhr,τbr,τ+ig2∑r,jhr,jbr,j,S=\sum_{r}\left[\frac{g_{\tau}^{2}}{2}(b_{r,\tau})^{2}+\frac{g^{2}}{2}\left((b_{r,x})^{2}+(b_{r,y})^{2}\right)\right]\\ {}+i\sum_{r}\left[A_{r,\tau}(\bar{\Delta}_{y}b_{r,x}-\bar{\Delta}_{x}b_{r,y})+A_{r,x}(\bar{\Delta}_{\tau}b_{r,y}-\bar{\Delta}_{y}b_{r,\tau})+A_{r,y}(\bar{\Delta}_{x}b_{r,\tau}-\bar{\Delta}_{\tau}b_{r,x})\right]\\ -2\pi i\sum_{r}m_{r}b_{r,\tau}+ig^{2}_{\tau}\sum_{r}h_{r,\tau}b_{r,\tau}+ig^{2}\sum_{r,j}h_{r,j}b_{r,j}, (S32)

where Δ¯μ​fr=fr−fr−μ^\bar{\Delta}_{\mu}f_{r}=f_{r}-f_{r-\hat{\mu}} denotes the backward difference operator, and mr∈ℤm_{r}\in\mathbb{Z} is integer-valued, so that the partition function now reads Z=∫ℝD[b]∫ℝD[A]∑{mr∈ℤ}e−SZ=\int_{\mathbb{R}}D[b]\int_{\mathbb{R}}D[A]\sum_{\{m_{r}\in\mathbb{Z}\}}e^{-S}. We may now integrate over the gauge-field variables AA, which act as Lagrange multipliers to enforce that br,ρb_{r,\rho} is flat, i.e. ϵμ​ν​ρ​Δ¯ν​br,ρ=0\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho}\bar{\Delta}_{\nu}b_{r,\rho}=0. We solve this constraint by writing br,ρ=Δ¯ρ​ϕrb_{r,\rho}=\bar{\Delta}_{\rho}\phi_{r} (note that we may write br,ρb_{r,\rho} globally as a gradient since any putative winding, i.e. topological defects, are now encoded in the explicit quantization of br,τb_{r,\tau} via the last term ∝mr​br,τ\propto m_{r}b_{r,\tau}).

Upon partially integrating the last term, we then arrive at the action

S=∑r[gτ22​(Δ¯τ​ϕr)2+g22​((Δ¯x​ϕr)2+(Δ¯y​ϕr)2)]+2​π​i​∑r(Δ¯τ​mr)​ϕr+i​∑r[gτ2​hr,τ​Δ¯τ​ϕr+g2​∑j=x,yhr,j​Δ¯j​ϕr].S=\sum_{r}\Big[\frac{g_{\tau}^{2}}{2}(\bar{\Delta}_{\tau}\phi_{r})^{2}+\frac{g^{2}}{2}\left((\bar{\Delta}_{x}\phi_{r})^{2}+(\bar{\Delta}_{y}\phi_{r})^{2}\right)\Big]+2\pi i\sum_{r}(\bar{\Delta}_{\tau}m_{r})\phi_{r}+i\sum_{r}\Big[g_{\tau}^{2}h_{r,\tau}\bar{\Delta}_{\tau}\phi_{r}+g^{2}\sum_{j=x,y}h_{r,j}\bar{\Delta}_{j}\phi_{r}\Big]. (S33)

with the associated partition function Z=∑{m∈ℤ}∫D[ϕ]e−SZ=\sum_{\{m\in\mathbb{Z}\}}\int D[\phi]e^{-S} (recall that hr,μh_{r,\mu} is a static background/source term). For a given configuration of mr∈ℤm_{r}\in\mathbb{Z}, the theory (S33) is a (discretized) action of a scalar field in 2+1-dims. which couples to integer variables Δ¯τ​mr∈ℤ\bar{\Delta}_{\tau}m_{r}\in\mathbb{Z}. While here we have index ϕr\phi_{r} with the sites of the space-time lattice, it is natural to associate the field ϕr\phi_{r} with the sites of the dual lattice (i.e. the centers of an elementary cube with a lower left front corner anchored at rr), and the field mrm_{r} with the horizontal (top/bottom) faces of such cube, such that Δ¯τ​mr\bar{\Delta}_{\tau}m_{r} lives on the cube centers, see also Fig. S5.

We now consider a given sector of winding variables krk_{r} in Eq. (S28). By varying with respect to hr,τh_{r,\tau} and hr,ih_{r,i} we obtain the flux on each plaquette as

Fr,τ≡Δx​Ar,y−Δy​Ar,x−2​π​kr\displaystyle F_{r,\tau}\equiv\Delta_{x}A_{r,y}-\Delta_{y}A_{r,x}-2\pi k_{r} =−i​gτ2​Δ¯τ​ϕr\displaystyle=-ig^{2}_{\tau}\bar{\Delta}_{\tau}\phi_{r} (S34a)
Fr,y≡Δτ​Ar,x−Δx​Ar,τ\displaystyle F_{r,y}\equiv\Delta_{\tau}A_{r,x}-\Delta_{x}A_{r,\tau} =−i​g2​Δ¯y​ϕr\displaystyle=-ig^{2}\bar{\Delta}_{y}\phi_{r} (S34b)
Fr,x≡Δy​Ar,τ−Δτ​Ar,y\displaystyle F_{r,x}\equiv\Delta_{y}A_{r,\tau}-\Delta_{\tau}A_{r,y} =−i​g2​Δ¯x​ϕr.\displaystyle=-ig^{2}\bar{\Delta}_{x}\phi_{r}. (S34c)

The left-hand side of the above expressions corresponds to the flux through the horizontal and vertical plaquettes of a cube anchored at rr. We may evaluate the total flux through the cube CC as a sum over the six (oriented) plaquettes as

∑p∈CFp​(−1)p=2​π​Δ¯τ​mr∈2​π​ℤ,\sum_{p\in C}F_{p}(-1)^{p}=2\pi\bar{\Delta}_{\tau}m_{r}\in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}, (S35)

where we have used a discrete version of the divergence theorem and the saddle-point equations of motion for ϕr\phi_{r}, i.e. gτ2​Δτ​Δ¯τ​ϕr+∑igi2​Δi​Δ¯i​ϕr=Δ¯τ​mrg_{\tau}^{2}\Delta_{\tau}\bar{\Delta}_{\tau}\phi_{r}+\sum_{i}g_{i}^{2}\Delta_{i}\bar{\Delta}_{i}\phi_{r}=\bar{\Delta}_{\tau}m_{r}.

VI.3 Discussion

From the above treatment, we draw three main conclusions:

  1. 1.

    The non-compact theory where the cos\cos in Eq. (S27) is replaced by a harmonic term, i.e. the sector with kr,τ≡0k_{r,\tau}\equiv 0 in Eq. (S28), features ∑p∈CFp​(−1)p≡0\sum_{p\in C}F_{p}(-1)^{p}\equiv 0: magnetic flux is conserved. There is an associated ℝ\mathbb{R}-symmetry which acts as ϕr→ϕr+c\phi_{r}\to\phi_{r}+c, c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} in the dual theory which becomes a free scalar field. The ground state breaks this symmetry spontaneously, and the linearly dispersing free scalar (Goldstone mode) yielding a dual description to the free photon.

  2. 2.

    In the theory (S27), flux only through spatial plaquettes (i.e. within a given time-slice) becomes compactified mod 2​π2\pi, as also evidenced by Eq. (S29). Is there an associated U(1)m flux conservation symmetry? Our explicit calculation, Eq. (S35) shows that there exist “monopole” configurations where integer multiples of 2​π2\pi flux emanate a space-time cube: one may define a corresponding monopole charge qr=Δ¯r​mrq_{r}=\bar{\Delta}_{r}m_{r}, and interpret the mrm_{r} variables as encoding the corresponding “Dirac string”. In contrast to usual (2+1)-dim. compact U(1) lattice gauge theory, these strings can only extend along the temporal direction as the 2​π2\pi windings on vertical plaquettes is heavily penalized by the harmonic terms in Eq. (S27). These monopole configurations explicitly spoil a putative U(1)m symmetry, as can also be seen from Eq. (S33): the dual scalar field gets pinned and loses the “shift” symmetry ϕ𝐫→ϕ𝐫+c\phi_{\bf r}\to\phi_{\bf r}+c.

  3. 3.

    We now consider the continuum limit δ​τ→0\delta\tau\to 0 along the imaginary-time (τ\tau) direction which amounts to scaling gτ2→gτ2/δ​τ→∞g_{\tau}^{2}\to g_{\tau}^{2}/\delta\tau\to\infty. In this limit, the kinetic term of the dual theory (S33) enjoys an (approximate) symmetry ϕr→ϕr+g⁡(x,y)\phi_{r}\to\phi_{r}+g(x,y), i.e. the field ϕr=ϕ⁡(x,y)\phi_{r}=\phi(x,y) is approximately time-independent. Then, the coupling ∑rΔ¯τ​mr​ϕr\sum_{r}\bar{\Delta}_{\tau}m_{r}\phi_{r} reduces to a boundary term in the temporal direction. Hence, the “monopole” term in Eq. (S33) vanishes (in the bulk). Thus, no confinement occurs: the shift symmetry of the scalar field ϕr\phi_{r} is restored, and it gives way to the (dual of the) gapless photon.

VII B=2B=2 DQMC and mean field spectra

We also investigate the spin structure factor inside the CF phase at B/t=2B/t=2 as shown in Fig. S3 and S4, comparing the results obtained with DQMC+SAC and mean-field methods. The B/t=2B/t=2 spin structure exhibits similar characteristics, featuring separate nearly dispersionless bands, akin to the findings for B/t=3B/t=3, as seen in Figs. 7 and 8. The Larmor mode in the transverse structure factor is located at ω=2​t=B\omega=2t=B. Notably, there is a significant reduction in spectral weight below the Larmor mode compared to the B/t=3B/t=3 case. The lower orbital magnetic field induced by B/t=2B/t=2 more closely resembles the scenario discussed in continuum field theory, where such reduced spectral weight below the Larmor mode is observed at small momenta, as shown in Fig. 6. Regarding the longitudinal structure factor, the DQMC spectra for J/t=0.1J/t=0.1 reveals a similar low-energy collective mode near 𝚪\mathbf{\Gamma}, also seen in B/t=3B/t=3 case, which is absent in mean-field results. These deviations from mean-field analysis might be attributed to gauge fluctuations discussed in Sec. IIC2.

VIII Finite size analysis of order parameters

Apart from the crossing point analysis in main text that manages to determine the transition points of CF and AFM phases, it is also worthwhile to do finite size analysis of CF and AFM order parameters. Namely study the scaling behavior of <fχ2><f^{2}_{\chi}> and S±​(𝐌)/L2S^{\pm}(\mathbf{M})/L^{2} versus 1/L1/L. Note that in the DQMC simulations, we already scale inverse temperature β\beta with 2​L2L to ensure that we are studying zero temperature physics. The finite size analysis results are shown in Fig. S6. The order parameters extrapolate to finite values inside long range ordered phase, whose boundaries are shown in the phase diagram, which is determined by crossing point analysis, in Fig.1(b) of the main text.
